course.title: Biology: Cells to Ecosystems
course.description: Explore a cell, follow its DNA and discover how living things shape a changing world.
course.audience: An adult comfortable with basic arithmetic and percentages. Build connected foundations in cells, genetics, evolution and ecology.

paragraphs: A leaf, a mouse and the bacteria in a spoonful of soil look about as different as living things can, yet each is built from cells, and every cell holds a copy of the instructions for making itself, written in DNA. Biology is the study of living things, and because they share that starting point, a handful of ideas about how a cell takes in what it needs, releases the energy in its food and copies its instructions go a long way towards explaining how a cut heals, why children resemble their parents without being copies of them, and how a population of moths can change colour over a few decades although no single moth ever does.

Much of the subject comes down to things you can count and measure. Comparing the concentration of dissolved substances on each side of a membrane tells you which way water will move and whether a cell will swell or shrink, working through the possible pairings of two parents' alleles gives the chance that an offspring shows a trait, and following the share of energy that passes from plants to the animals that eat them explains why a field holds so many more plants than foxes. Claims about living things are judged in the same way, by asking what was measured and what it was compared with.
outcomes: You'll be able to tell a bacterium from an animal or plant cell and say what each main part does.
You'll be able to predict which way water and dissolved substances move across a membrane.
You'll be able to follow energy and carbon through a leaf and through a cell that uses fuel.
You'll be able to work out the chance that offspring inherit a trait from a simple cross.
You'll be able to read a food web and calculate how much energy reaches each level.
introduction.prerequisites: You should be comfortable with basic arithmetic and percentages; no biology is assumed.

lessons.title: A world inside a cell

lead.text: Whatever its size, a cell has to stay separate from its surroundings and still take in food and give out waste. The structure that makes both possible is a thin film around the whole cell called the **plasma membrane**, which is built from two layers of fatty molecules with larger molecules set into them. It works like a doorkeeper, because oxygen and water cross it easily while many other substances can pass only through specific carrier molecules in the membrane, or *not at all*.

The figure shows an animal cell and a bacterium, and the outline picked out in gold on each is the plasma membrane. Both cells have one, as does every other living cell, so the membrane is a feature that **all cells share** and cannot be used to tell them apart.

afterFigure.text: The watery interior that the membrane encloses is the **cytoplasm**, a mixture of dissolved substances in which the cell's chemical reactions take place and its other parts are suspended.

lead.text: A cell also needs instructions, and these are carried by **DNA**, a long molecule whose sequence of chemical units spells out how to make each of the cell's proteins, the large molecules that do most of its work. An animal cell packs most of its DNA into a **nucleus**, a compartment of its own wrapped in a membrane, and any cell built this way is called **eukaryotic**, from the Greek for "true kernel". Plant and animal cells are both *eukaryotic*.

A bacterium has no nucleus. Its DNA, usually a single circular molecule, lies coiled in one region of the cytoplasm called the **nucleoid**, which has no membrane around it, so the instructions and everything else share the same open space.

afterFigure.text: Switch between the two cells and compare where the purple material sits: inside a rounded nucleus in the animal cell, and as a loose coil in the bacterium. This is the clearest single difference between the two designs.

lead.text: Suspended in the cytoplasm of a eukaryotic cell are structures called **organelles**, each of which has its own job. The **mitochondria** are rod-shaped organelles that release energy from fuel such as sugar and make it available for the cell's work, which is why cells that use a great deal of energy are packed with them. **Ribosomes** are tiny structures that build [[proteins|The large molecules that do most of a cell's work. Met earlier in this lesson.]] by reading instructions copied from the DNA and joining the building blocks in the right order.

afterFigure.text: The ribosomes are drawn only in the bacterium, as a row of dots, so that they can be seen, but eukaryotic cells have them too, in very large numbers. Every cell has to make proteins, and so every cell has ribosomes, whereas mitochondria are a *eukaryotic* feature.

lead.text: A plant makes its own food from light, and the cells of a leaf have an organelle that carries out the first stage: the **chloroplast**. Chloroplasts contain the green pigment chlorophyll, which absorbs light, and they use that energy to build sugar from carbon dioxide and water in a process called photosynthesis.

afterFigure.text: The leaf cell in the figure has chloroplasts in addition to everything an animal cell has. Chloroplasts appear only in cells that are **exposed to light**, so a root cell underground has none, and it depends on sugar made in the leaves and carried down to it.

lead.text: The leaf cell in the figure has one more layer than the animal cell, a firm **cell wall** that lies outside the plasma membrane. In plants the wall is built mainly from cellulose, and it works like a rigid frame, giving the cell its shape and resisting the pressure of the water inside it. Most bacteria are also surrounded by a wall, made of a different material, while animal cells have none.

afterFigure.text: The wall does not take over the membrane's work. It is porous, so substances pass through it freely, and the [[plasma membrane|The thin film around every cell that controls what enters and leaves. Met earlier in this lesson.]] just inside it remains **the layer that decides what enters and leaves**. Robert Hooke's cork cells were exactly these walls, left standing after the living contents had gone, which is why he saw empty boxes.

lessons.orientation: The parts every cell shares, what a nucleus, mitochondria, chloroplast and cell wall add, and how a bacterium differs from an animal or plant cell.

blocks.text: In 1665 Robert Hooke cut a thin slice of cork, put it under a microscope and saw that it was divided into rows of tiny box-shaped compartments, which he called *cells* because they reminded him of the small rooms in a monastery.

Cells differ greatly in size. A bacterium such as *Escherichia coli* is about two micrometres long, while a typical animal cell measures 10 to 20 micrometres across. Inside that small space each cell holds a boundary, a store of instructions and the machinery to use fuel, and it arranges them in one of two basic ways.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to tell a bacterium from an animal or plant cell and say what each main part does.
intro.whyItMatters: Every later lesson happens inside a cell or between cells, so these parts and their jobs are the vocabulary for the rest of the course.

recap.keyIdea: Every cell has a plasma membrane and DNA, a eukaryotic cell keeps its DNA in a nucleus and has organelles with set jobs, and a bacterium has neither.

blocks.text: Every cell is enclosed by a **plasma membrane** that controls what enters and leaves, and every cell carries DNA and makes proteins on ribosomes. A **eukaryotic** cell encloses its DNA in a nucleus and divides its work among organelles such as mitochondria, which release energy from fuel, while a bacterium keeps its DNA in an open nucleoid and has no mitochondria.
A leaf cell adds chloroplasts, which capture light, and a cell wall outside the membrane that supports it, so its parts follow from the jobs it must do.

lessons.title: Which way will molecules move?

lead.text: Take two compartments of equal size, joined by a membrane that a dissolved substance can cross, and put 16 units of the substance on the left and 4 on the right, where a unit stands for a fixed number of molecules. Because the volumes are equal, the left side has the higher **concentration**, meaning that it holds more of the substance in the same space.

Every molecule moves at random, and one beside the membrane is as likely to cross to the right as to the left. There are simply *more* of them on the left, so in any short time more molecules cross from left to right than back again. The result is a **net movement** from the side of higher concentration to the side of lower concentration, which is called **diffusion**.

afterFigure.text: Move the slider under the figure and the left count falls while the right count rises, until the two are equal. Diffusion needs no energy from the cell, because it is driven only by the random motion that molecules already have.

lead.text: Net movement lasts only while one side holds more than the other. Each molecule that leaves the crowded side arrives on the other, so the gap between the sides shrinks until the two have the same [[concentration|The amount of a substance in a given space. Met earlier in this lesson.]], a state called **equilibrium**.

Since molecules are moved from one side to the other and never created or destroyed, **the total stays the same throughout**. With equal volumes, equilibrium therefore has a simple form: each side holds half of the total.

afterFigure.text: In the first case of the figure the total is 17 + 5 = 22 units, so each side finishes with 22 ÷ 2 = 11. The second case starts from the opposite arrangement, 6 + 16 = 22, and finishes at the same place. The final amounts depend on the total and on the volumes, but not on which side began with more.

lead.text: [[Equilibrium|The state in which the concentrations on the two sides are equal. Met earlier in this lesson.]] does not mean that the molecules have stopped. Each one is still moving at random and still crossing the membrane from time to time, but with equal concentrations on the two sides, *as many* cross from left to right as from right to left. The counts therefore stay the same even though the movement goes on, which is what is meant by saying that there is **no net movement**, only movement in both directions.

afterFigure.text: The total gives a useful check on any working. If the amounts on the two sides at equilibrium do not add up to the amount you began with, a unit has been lost somewhere in the counting.

lead.text: So far the solute could always cross, but a cell's plasma membrane does not let everything through. It is **selectively permeable**: small uncharged molecules such as oxygen and carbon dioxide slip between its fatty molecules, water also crosses, and larger molecules and ions, which are atoms or molecules carrying an electric charge, cross only through specific proteins in the membrane, or not at all. A membrane is **permeable** to a substance when that substance can cross it, and **impermeable** when it cannot.

This decides whether diffusion happens. If the membrane is permeable to the solute, the amounts shift by [[diffusion|The net movement of a substance from higher to lower concentration. Met earlier in this lesson.]] as in the earlier figures. If it is impermeable, *no* molecule crosses, so neither side can gain or lose any and each keeps the amount it started with, however large the difference in concentration.

afterFigure.text: In the figure's second case the barrier lets nothing through, so the counts stay at 14 and 6 however far the slider is moved.

lessons.orientation: How random motion makes a dissolved substance spread from higher to lower concentration, where it settles, and how permeability changes the outcome.

blocks.text: In 1827 the botanist Robert Brown watched pollen grains suspended in water through a microscope and saw them jitter about without pause, as if each were being pushed by something invisible. The cause was not settled until 1905, when Albert Einstein showed that the grains were being struck from every side by water molecules, which are themselves in **constant, random motion**.

That restless motion is what moves dissolved substances around and into cells. A single molecule has no sense of where it is going, yet when many of them are packed more densely in one place than in another, their random movements alone produce a steady drift with a direction you can predict.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to predict which way a dissolved substance moves across a membrane and how much ends up on each side.
intro.whyItMatters: Cells take in nutrients and lose waste by this movement, so predicting its direction is the first step in understanding how a cell stays supplied.

recap.keyIdea: Dissolved substances diffuse from higher to lower concentration until the sides are equal, and a membrane that blocks a substance stops the movement.

blocks.text: Because molecules move at random, more cross from the side of higher concentration than from the side of lower, so there is a net movement down the gradient called **diffusion**. It continues until the concentrations are equal, and with equal volumes that means each side holds half of the total, while the molecules themselves keep crossing in both directions at the same rate.
A membrane that is **impermeable** to a substance stops its diffusion altogether, so each side keeps the amount it started with.

recap.nextHook: Water crosses a membrane even when the dissolved substance cannot, and the next lesson asks which way it goes when only water can cross.

lessons.title: When only water can cross

lead.text: The amount of a dissolved substance, the solute, is not the same quantity as its concentration. **Concentration** is the amount of solute divided by the volume of the solution, so 9 units of solute in a volume of 3 have a concentration of 3 units per volume, while the same 9 units in a volume of 9 have a concentration of only 1.

When water is added to a solution and no solute is added, the same amount is spread through a larger volume, and the solution is *diluted*. **The amount of solute can stay fixed while the concentration changes**, and this distinction decides which way water moves across a membrane.

Now suppose the membrane is [[permeable|Letting a substance cross. Met in 'Which way will molecules move?'.]] to water but not to the solute, which is true of a cell membrane and a large dissolved molecule. The solute cannot move, so the equalising has to be done by the water. Water also moves by diffusion, from where it is more concentrated to where it is less, and the side with more solute has proportionally *less* water in the same space, so water diffuses into it.

The net movement of water across a [[selectively permeable|Letting some substances cross and holding others back. Met in 'Which way will molecules move?'.]] membrane towards the side with the higher solute concentration is called **osmosis**. As the slider moves, water crosses, the partition shifts, and the side that gained water grows while the other shrinks.

afterFigure.text: The movement ends when the two concentrations are equal. In the first case the left side begins with 3 units and the right with 15, so the right side draws in water until the volumes are in the same ratio as the solute, one to five, and the concentrations match. The amount of solute on each side never changes, only the volume it is dissolved in.

lead.text: To follow what water movement does to a compartment, keep two things apart. The **amount** of solute stays fixed, because none can cross, and the **volume** changes as water enters or leaves, so the new concentration is always the same fixed amount divided by the new volume.

Each compartment starts with a volume of 1, so the left concentration is 3 ÷ 1 = 3 and the right is 15 ÷ 1 = 15. The total of 18 units shared through a total volume of 2 gives an equal concentration of 18 ÷ 2 = 9 at the end, which needs a left volume of one third (3 ÷ 9) and a right volume of one and two thirds (15 ÷ 9). Water has therefore left the left side, whose concentration *rises* from 3 to 9, and entered the right, whose concentration *falls* from 15 to 9.

A plant cell sits in a watery environment, and its cytoplasm usually holds more dissolved substances than the water outside, so water tends to enter by [[osmosis|The net movement of water across a membrane towards the side with more solute. Met earlier in this lesson.]]. A plant cell cannot burst so easily, because the [[cell wall|The firm layer outside a plant cell's plasma membrane. Met in 'A world inside a cell'.]] around it is *rigid*.

As water enters, the cell swells and presses against the wall, and the wall presses back. This push, called **turgor pressure**, grows until it opposes the tendency of water to enter, at which point net entry stops. The cell is then firm, and a plant that loses water through its leaves loses this pressure and wilts.

lessons.orientation: How to tell concentration from amount, and how water moves across a membrane that the solute cannot cross.

blocks.text: In 1748 the French physicist Jean-Antoine Nollet filled a jar with spirit of wine, tied a pig's bladder over its mouth and stood the jar in water. The bladder swelled outward as water passed in through it, and this is generally cited as the first recorded observation of a **membrane passing water while holding back what was dissolved in the jar**.

The plasma membrane of a cell behaves in a similar way, passing water far more readily than most of the substances dissolved in the cell, and the water that crosses it decides whether the cell swells, shrinks or stays firm.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to predict which way water moves across a membrane that a solute cannot cross, and work out the new concentration.
intro.whyItMatters: Water balance decides whether a cell swells, shrinks or stays firm, and it explains why plants wilt.

recap.keyIdea: Water moves towards the side with the higher solute concentration when the solute cannot cross, and a cell wall can stop the entry by pressing back.

blocks.text: **Concentration** is the amount of solute divided by the volume, so when the solute cannot cross, its amount stays fixed while its concentration changes with the volume. [[Diffusion|The net movement of a substance from higher to lower concentration. Met in 'Which way will molecules move?'.]] of water towards the side with more solute is **osmosis**, and it continues until the concentrations are equal.
In a plant cell the wall pushes back as the cell swells, and this turgor pressure can bring net entry of water to a halt.

lessons.title: Make a reaction easier

lead.text: Even a reaction that releases energy overall does not start by itself, because the molecules must first be pushed into an unstable arrangement before they can rearrange into something else. The energy needed for that push is called the **activation energy**, and it is the reason sugar and oxygen can sit together in a bowl for years without reacting. A **catalyst** is a substance that speeds up a reaction by lowering this barrier, and the catalysts that living things make are the **enzymes**, which are proteins.

An enzyme does not supply energy, and it does not change what is made. It offers a route with a lower barrier, and it comes out of the reaction unchanged, so a single enzyme molecule can work on one batch after another. The substance it acts on is its **substrate**, and what it produces are the **products**.

afterFigure.text: The beaker with the enzyme makes 15 units of product each minute against 5 without it, so it is three times as fast, and it forms the same product. The enzyme has changed *how fast* the reaction goes and nothing else.

lead.text: The enzyme in the figure on the previous screen made the same product, only faster.

An enzyme is a large, folded protein, and on its surface is a small pocket whose shape and chemistry match its substrate. This pocket is the **active site**. The [[substrate|The substance an enzyme acts on. Met earlier in this lesson.]] binds there, the enzyme helps it rearrange into products, the products leave, and the active site is free to take the next substrate. Because the fit depends on exact shape, each enzyme works on only one substrate or a few closely related ones: the enzyme in saliva that breaks down starch has no effect on proteins.

afterFigure.text: Emil Fischer proposed in 1894 that substrate and enzyme fit together like a key in a lock. Since Daniel Koshland suggested the idea of *induced fit* in 1958, the active site has been understood to adjust its shape slightly as the substrate binds, but the central point remains: **the shape of the active site decides what the enzyme can do**.

lead.text: Raising the temperature makes molecules move faster, so [[enzyme|A protein that speeds up a reaction by lowering its activation energy. Met earlier in this lesson.]] and substrate meet more often and with more energy, and the rate of the reaction rises. The rise does not continue, because an enzyme is held in its folded shape by weak attractions, and at higher temperatures these break. The enzyme unfolds, the [[active site|The pocket on an enzyme where the substrate binds. Met earlier in this lesson.]] loses its *shape*, and the substrate no longer fits, a change called **denaturation** that usually cannot be undone.

The temperature at which an enzyme's rate is highest is its **optimum**, and it differs between enzymes. Human enzymes generally work best near body temperature, 37°C, while a bacterium living in a hot spring has enzymes that keep working at well over 70°C.

afterFigure.text: In the figure, Enzyme C rises to a peak at 25°C and then falls, because it is being denatured, while Enzyme B is still climbing at 55°C, so its optimum lies above anything measured here.

lead.text: Add more substrate to a fixed amount of enzyme and the rate rises at first, because at any moment more active sites find a substrate. Eventually every active site is occupied, and the extra substrate has to wait for a site to come free, so the rate levels off at a maximum. At that point **the enzyme has become the limiting factor**, and the only way to raise the rate further is to add more enzyme, which supplies more active sites.

afterFigure.text: The line for the fixed amount of enzyme in the figure rises from 2 to 7 as the substrate goes from 1 to 4, but when the substrate doubles again, from 4 to 8, the rate gains only 1. The line for more enzyme keeps climbing over the same range, from 8 to 14, because it has more sites to fill.

lead.text: To show that an enzyme is responsible for a change, you need two samples that are alike in every respect but one: a sample with the enzyme added, and a **control** without it, matched in temperature, amount of substrate, volume and time. Whatever difference then appears can be put down to the enzyme, because nothing else differs. A single pair of samples can mislead, so a careful experiment is **replicated**, meaning it is repeated with several samples, and a difference is trusted only if it is larger than the variation among the replicates.

afterFigure.text: In the figure, the sample with the enzyme has made 21 units of product after 3 minutes and its matched control has made 6. The control shows what forms without the enzyme, so the enzyme can be credited only with the difference, 21 − 6 = 15 units.

lessons.orientation: How an enzyme lowers a reaction's energy barrier, what changes its rate, and how to design a fair test of its effect.

blocks.text: In 1897 the German chemist Eduard Buchner ground yeast cells with sand, pressed out the juice, and found that with no living cell left in it the juice still turned sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide. Fermentation had been thought to need life itself, and Buchner's result showed that it needs only certain substances made by the cell, which Wilhelm Kühne had named *enzymes* in 1877.
A cell's chemistry depends on enzymes because most of its reactions, left alone, would run far too slowly to keep it alive, and an enzyme can speed one up by many millions of times.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to explain how an enzyme speeds a reaction, read rate data and say whether an experiment is a fair test.
intro.whyItMatters: Nearly every reaction in a cell depends on an enzyme, and the same fair-test reasoning is how biologists decide what caused a result.

recap.keyIdea: An enzyme speeds a reaction by lowering its activation energy, its rate depends on temperature and the number of active sites, and a control shows what the enzyme earns.

blocks.text: An **enzyme** is a protein whose [[active site|The pocket on an enzyme where the substrate binds. Met earlier in this lesson.]] fits its substrate and lowers the activation energy, so the reaction runs faster and the enzyme is left unchanged. Heat speeds it up until the protein is denatured, and when every active site is busy, the enzyme limits the rate and more substrate changes nothing.
To credit a change to the enzyme, compare matched, replicated samples that differ only in whether the enzyme was added, and take the difference from the **control**.

recap.nextHook: Enzymes also drive the reactions by which a leaf builds sugar from light, and the next lesson follows the carbon through that process.

lessons.title: Where does a leaf get its carbon?

lead.text: A leaf takes in carbon dioxide from the air through tiny pores in its surface and draws up water from the roots. In its chloroplasts it uses the energy of light to join the carbon from the carbon dioxide into **glucose**, a sugar whose molecule has six carbon atoms, and the oxygen left over is released into the air. This whole process is called **photosynthesis**.

The equation is a summary of many separate steps, each helped by an enzyme, but it gives the totals correctly: for every glucose molecule that is made, six molecules of carbon dioxide and six of water are used up and six molecules of oxygen are released.

afterFigure.text: Doubling the glucose doubles every amount in the equation, because each product is built from a fixed number of the inputs.

lead.text: The equation can be read as a count of atoms. A carbon dioxide molecule holds exactly one carbon atom, and a [[glucose|A sugar whose molecule has six carbon atoms. Met earlier in this lesson.]] molecule holds six, so **each glucose must be built from six carbon dioxide molecules**, and a leaf that makes 10 glucose molecules must take in 60 carbon dioxide molecules. The atoms are rearranged and never made or lost, so the carbon that goes in as gas comes out as sugar.

This was confirmed in the late 1940s and 1950s, when Melvin Calvin and his colleagues gave green algae carbon dioxide containing radioactive carbon-14 and followed the *labelled* carbon as it appeared first in a series of intermediate compounds and then in sugars. The method worked because the leaf cannot tell labelled carbon atoms from ordinary ones, so wherever the label turns up is where the carbon went.

The inputs do two different jobs. Carbon dioxide and water are *matter*: their atoms end up in glucose and oxygen, which is why a plant's mass comes from them and not from the soil. Light is *energy*, and it has no atoms to add. Chlorophyll in the [[chloroplast|The organelle in a leaf cell that absorbs light and builds sugar. Met in 'A world inside a cell'.]] absorbs it, and the energy is stored in the bonds of the glucose as **chemical energy**, a form that can be kept until a cell needs it.

In 1779 Jan Ingenhousz found that plants release oxygen only in the light, and only from their green parts. In 1941 Samuel Ruben and Martin Kamen supplied algae with water that contained a heavy form of oxygen and found that the heavy oxygen came off as gas, which shows that **the oxygen released comes from the water** and not from the carbon dioxide.

[[Photosynthesis|The process by which a leaf builds glucose from carbon dioxide and water using light. Met earlier in this lesson.]] needs light, carbon dioxide and a suitable temperature, and the slowest of these requirements sets the pace. The one that is in shortest supply at the moment is the **limiting factor**.

afterFigure.text: Both curves in the figure match up to a light level of 20, where light is limiting for each leaf. Beyond that the leaf with less carbon dioxide levels off at a rate of 10, because it has run short of carbon dioxide and cannot use the extra light, while the leaf with more carbon dioxide keeps rising to 18. A flat part of a curve is therefore the place where another factor has taken over as the limit.

lessons.orientation: How a leaf turns carbon dioxide, water and light into glucose and oxygen, where the atoms and the energy go, and what limits the rate.
lessons.reviewLabel: Where does a leaf get its carbon?
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: In the first half of the seventeenth century the Flemish physician Jan Baptist van Helmont weighed 200 pounds of dried soil into a pot, planted in it a willow shoot weighing 5 pounds, and for five years gave it nothing but water. At the end the willow weighed about 169 pounds, while the soil, dried and weighed again, had lost only about 2 ounces. Van Helmont concluded that the new wood had been made from water.

He was right that water mattered, but it cannot be the whole story, because about half of the dry mass of wood is *carbon* and water contains none, so **the carbon must have come from the air**. A leaf takes it in and joins it into sugar with the energy of sunlight, which makes this process, photosynthesis, the point where the matter and the energy of almost every food chain begin.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to trace carbon and energy through photosynthesis and use its overall equation to count molecules.
intro.whyItMatters: Nearly all the food and oxygen on land comes from this one process, so it sets the starting point for every food chain.

recap.keyIdea: A leaf builds glucose from carbon dioxide and water using the energy of light, and the sugar's carbon atoms all come from carbon dioxide.

blocks.text: **Photosynthesis** joins six carbon dioxide and six water molecules into one glucose and six oxygen, so each glucose holds six carbon atoms that all came from carbon dioxide. The two inputs supply the matter, while light supplies the energy, which is stored in the glucose as chemical energy.
The rate is set by the [[limiting factor|The requirement in shortest supply, which sets the rate. Met earlier in this lesson.]], and a flat part of a curve shows where another factor has taken over.

recap.nextHook: The chemical energy stored in glucose is what a cell releases when it uses fuel, and the next lesson follows the carbon and the energy through that reaction.

lessons.title: How does a cell use its fuel?

lead.text: A cell gets its energy by breaking [[glucose|The sugar a leaf builds, with six carbon atoms in each molecule. Met in 'Where does a leaf get its carbon?'.]] down in the presence of oxygen, a process called **cellular respiration**. The atoms of glucose and oxygen are rearranged into carbon dioxide and water, and the change can be written as an equation that is the *reverse* of the one for photosynthesis.

Burning glucose in a flame would give the same products, but all of its energy would be released at once as heat. A cell avoids this by spreading the breakdown over many small steps, each controlled by an enzyme, the first in the cytoplasm and the last in the [[mitochondria|Organelles that release energy from fuel for the cell to use. Met in 'A world inside a cell'.]], so that the energy comes out in pieces a cell can use.

afterFigure.text: What photosynthesis builds, respiration takes apart, and the same six molecules of carbon dioxide, water and oxygen appear in each, in opposite roles.

lead.text: The energy released from glucose is not used on the spot. Part of it is transferred to a small molecule called **ATP**, short for adenosine triphosphate, which carries it to wherever the cell has work to do. When ATP delivers its energy it is turned into a similar molecule with one phosphate group fewer, and [[cellular respiration|The reactions in a cell that release the energy of fuel using oxygen. Met earlier in this lesson.]] then rebuilds it, so the same molecules are used again and again.

Not all of the energy from the glucose reaches ATP, because the transfers are not perfectly efficient. **Well under half of it is captured, and the rest disperses as heat**, which is why an active animal feels warm.

Every carbon atom in a glucose molecule is still there at the end, because atoms are rearranged in a reaction and *never* lost. A glucose molecule has six of them, and carbon dioxide takes one atom each, so **each glucose breaks down into six carbon dioxide molecules**. A cell that breaks down three glucose molecules therefore produces 18 carbon dioxide molecules, and carries all 18 carbon atoms away.

afterFigure.text: The carbon dioxide is carried away in the blood and breathed out, and a plant takes it back in and builds it into sugar again, so the carbon moves in a cycle between sugar and the air.

lead.text: **Breathing** is the movement of air into and out of the lungs, which brings oxygen close to the blood and removes carbon dioxide. **Cellular respiration** is the set of chemical reactions in each cell that releases the energy of fuel, and it needs the oxygen that breathing brings.

Respiration is not limited to animals. A plant respires in every living cell, day and night, and photosynthesises only in the light, and yeast and bacteria respire too. Some cells can also release a little energy without oxygen, as yeast does when it ferments sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide, but this yields much less energy from each glucose than respiration with oxygen does.
Because respiration uses oxygen, the rate at which oxygen disappears from a sealed jar of living organisms measures how fast they are respiring.

A reading alone can mislead, because oxygen can fall for reasons that have nothing to do with the organisms, such as a slow leak or some of the gas dissolving in water. A **blank** jar, set up in the same way but with no organisms, shows how much of the change happens anyway. **The organisms' own use is the change in their jar minus the change in the blank.**

afterFigure.text: In the figure, the jar of organisms falls from 24 to 18 units in three minutes, a loss of 6, while the blank falls from 24 to 23, a loss of 1. The organisms therefore used 6 − 1 = 5 units, and the blank explains the other 1.

lessons.orientation: How a cell releases the energy of glucose with oxygen, where the carbon goes, what ATP does, and how to measure respiration.
lessons.reviewLabel: How does a cell use its fuel?
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: In the 1780s Antoine Lavoisier and Pierre-Simon Laplace put a guinea pig in a chamber packed with ice and measured how much of the ice melted, which gave the heat the animal produced, and they compared this with the carbon dioxide it breathed out. The two stood in about the same proportion as when charcoal burns, and they concluded that **respiration is a slow form of burning**.
The comparison was sound, although the burning was first thought to take place in the lungs, and it is now known to go on in every living cell.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to follow carbon and energy through cellular respiration and keep it apart from breathing.
intro.whyItMatters: Every cell, in you and in a plant, depends on respiration for its energy, and the oxygen you breathe is used in it.

recap.keyIdea: Respiration breaks glucose down with oxygen into carbon dioxide and water, transferring part of the energy to ATP and the rest to heat.

blocks.text: In **cellular respiration** a cell rearranges glucose and oxygen into carbon dioxide and water, so every carbon atom of the fuel leaves in a carbon dioxide molecule. Part of the energy released is carried by **ATP** to the cell's work, and the rest disperses as heat.
Breathing only moves air to and from the lungs, and respiration goes on in the cells of plants and animals alike, which is why oxygen use in a sealed jar, corrected by a blank, measures it.

recap.nextHook: The enzymes that run all this chemistry are built from instructions written in DNA, and the next lesson shows how a cell copies that message one base at a time.

lessons.title: Copy a message one base at a time

lead.text: A DNA molecule consists of two long strands wound around each other. Each strand is a chain of units, and each unit carries one of four chemical groups called **bases**, named adenine, thymine, cytosine and guanine and abbreviated A, T, C and G. The strands are held together by weak attractions between bases that face each other across the gap, and these form *only* between particular pairs, which are A with T and C with G.

Because the bases in each pair match, the two strands are said to be **complementary**, and the rule that fixes the partners is called complementary base pairing. In about 1950 Erwin Chargaff had found that the DNA of every species he tested contains as much A as T and as much C as G, a regularity that the pairing rule explains.

afterFigure.text: The upper strand in the figure is the one given, and the lower strand shows its partners as the slider moves. **A is always across from T and C is always across from G**, never any other way round.

lead.text: Because every base has *exactly one* partner, the order of [[bases|The four chemical groups carried by the units of a DNA strand: A, T, C and G. Met earlier in this lesson.]] along one strand tells you the order along the other. A strand reading GATC must be paired with one reading CTAG, found by taking each base in turn: G with C, A with T, T with A and C with G. The two strands also run in opposite directions, which is why the figure labels the left end of the upper strand 5′ and the left end of the lower strand 3′, the names of the two ends of each strand.

This is what makes copying possible. Either strand can act as a **template**, a pattern along which its partner is built, and the partner built against it will always come out in the same order as the strand it replaces.

Before a cell divides it must copy all of its DNA. Enzymes unwind the double helix and separate its two strands, and then each strand serves as a [[template|A strand used as a pattern along which its partner is built. Met earlier in this lesson.]]. Free bases are matched to the template *one at a time*, A to T and C to G, and an enzyme called DNA polymerase joins them into a new strand. When the work is done there are two DNA molecules, and each consists of one old strand and one newly built strand.

This is called **semiconservative replication**, because each new molecule conserves half of the old one. In 1958 Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl showed that it is what really happens, by growing bacteria in a heavy form of nitrogen, moving them to ordinary nitrogen and measuring the density of their DNA after each copying.

afterFigure.text: The strand built in the figure is entirely new, and it stays paired with the old template it was built on. The other old strand gets a new partner in the same way, so one molecule becomes **two molecules, each half old and half new**.

lead.text: In a eukaryotic cell the DNA is divided among several long molecules, each packaged with proteins into a **chromosome**. Before copying, each chromosome holds a single DNA molecule. When it is copied, the two new molecules stay attached to each other, and the pair is still counted as one chromosome, but each half is now called a **sister chromatid**.

Counting therefore needs care. A cell with 3 chromosomes has 3 DNA molecules before copying and 6 afterwards, since each chromosome now holds two, yet it still has 3 chromosomes. *Copying doubles the number of DNA molecules and leaves the number of chromosomes unchanged.*

afterFigure.text: The figure shows a cell with two chromosomes. Before copying it has 2 chromosomes and 2 DNA molecules, and after copying it has the same 2 chromosomes, each drawn as two joined chromatids, which makes 4 DNA molecules.

lessons.orientation: How complementary base pairing lets each strand of DNA act as a template, and how copying changes the numbers of DNA molecules and chromosomes.
lessons.reviewLabel: Copy a message one base at a time
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: On 25 April 1953 James Watson and Francis Crick published a one-page paper in the journal *Nature* describing the double helix of DNA, and ended it with a sentence famous for its understatement: "It has not escaped our notice that the specific pairing we have postulated immediately suggests a possible copying mechanism for the genetic material."

DNA is a double strand in which each unit has **one fixed partner**, so that either strand carries what is needed to rebuild the other, and copying a molecule millions of units long becomes a matter of matching partners one at a time.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to write the partner of a DNA strand and count DNA molecules and chromosomes before and after copying.
intro.whyItMatters: A cell copies all of its DNA before every division, and this pairing rule is why the copy is accurate.

recap.keyIdea: A pairs with T and C pairs with G, so each strand is a template for its partner, and copying doubles the DNA molecules but not the chromosomes.

blocks.text: In DNA, **complementary base pairing** gives every base one partner, A with T and C with G, so each old strand serves as a template for a new one, and the result is two molecules that each keep one old strand, in **semiconservative replication**.

Copying leaves the number of chromosomes unchanged and doubles the number of DNA molecules, because the two [[sister chromatids|The two identical, joined copies of a replicated chromosome. Met earlier in this lesson.]] of a chromosome are counted together.

recap.nextHook: The two chromatids of each copied chromosome are pulled apart when a cell divides, and the next lesson follows that sharing out in mitosis.

lessons.title: Make two cells

lead.text: Mitosis comes after the DNA has been copied, when each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids. During **mitosis** the chromosomes line up across the middle of the cell, and a set of protein fibres called the spindle pulls the two chromatids of every chromosome to opposite ends. Once they have separated, each chromatid is counted as a chromosome in its own right, so both ends of the cell receive a complete set, and a nucleus re-forms around each.

The cell then divides its cytoplasm in a step called **cytokinesis**, which in an animal cell is a pinching of the membrane and in a plant cell the building of a new wall across the middle. The result is two **daughter cells**.

afterFigure.text: **Mitosis keeps the chromosome number the same and makes two cells whose DNA is identical**, apart from the rare copying mistakes of a later lesson.

lead.text: A cell spends most of its life between divisions, in a stage called **interphase**, when it grows and copies its DNA. Mitosis and cytokinesis are the shorter part of the *cell cycle* in which the copies are shared out. The order matters for counting, because the number of DNA molecules changes twice while the number of chromosomes in the cell stays the same.

Take a human cell, which has 46 chromosomes. Before copying it has 46 DNA molecules. After copying it still has 46 chromosomes, but each now holds two DNA molecules, so there are 92. When the sister chromatids separate, each daughter cell receives 46 chromosomes holding one DNA molecule each, which is 46 DNA molecules, the same as the cell began with. The count of DNA molecules therefore *doubles* when the DNA is copied and *halves* when the cell divides.

One cell divides into two, and each of those into two more, so **the number of cells doubles with every round**. After five rounds, then, there are 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32 cells, and after *n* rounds there are 2 multiplied by itself *n* times.

Doubling grows quickly. A human adult is estimated to have 30 to 40 trillion cells, and a fertilised egg would reach about 35 trillion after only 45 rounds of doubling, although in reality cells divide at different rates and many are lost along the way.

Cells do not divide at random. A fertilised egg divides again and again by [[mitosis|The division that shares copied chromosomes equally between two daughter cells. Met earlier in this lesson.]] to become an embryo, a child grows because its cells multiply, and in an adult division replaces cells that wear out, such as those of the skin and the lining of the gut. Other cells, such as most nerve cells in the brain, hardly divide at all.

Division is therefore controlled, and cancer is what follows when the control fails and a cell divides without limit. Because only some cells in a tissue divide in a given round, counting needs a little care: **a cell that divides becomes two, and a cell that does not divide stays one**, so the two groups are counted separately and then added.

lessons.orientation: How mitosis shares a copied set of chromosomes between two daughter cells, how the DNA and cell counts change, and why cells divide.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: In 1855 Rudolf Virchow wrote that every cell arises from a cell that already existed, in the Latin phrase *omnis cellula e cellula*. In 1882 Walther Flemming, who had stained dividing cells from salamander larvae and watched the threads in their nuclei shorten, split lengthwise and move apart, named the process *mitosis*, from the Greek for thread.

What Flemming watched is how **one cell becomes two that are identical in their DNA**, and it is the division by which a fertilised egg becomes a body, a cut heals and a plant grows. Each of those depends on every new cell receiving a full set of instructions.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to follow chromosomes through mitosis and count the DNA molecules and the cells that result.
intro.whyItMatters: Growth, healing and the replacement of worn-out cells all depend on cells dividing accurately, and counting them shows how fast that can go.

recap.keyIdea: Mitosis shares the copied chromosomes equally, so each daughter cell has the same number as the parent, and repeated rounds double the number of cells.

blocks.text: In **mitosis** the [[sister chromatids|The two identical, joined copies of a replicated chromosome. Met in 'Copy a message one base at a time'.]] of each chromosome are pulled to opposite ends of the cell, and cytokinesis then divides the cell into two daughters with the same chromosome number and identical DNA. The number of DNA molecules doubles when DNA is copied and halves when the cell divides.
Every round of division doubles the number of cells, so one cell gives 8 after three rounds, and when only some cells divide, the dividing and non-dividing cells are counted separately.

recap.nextHook: Mitosis makes cells that are identical to their parent, and the next lesson asks how a different kind of division makes the sex cells that carry only half the chromosomes.

lessons.title: Halve a chromosome set

lead.text: A human body cell has 46 chromosomes, and they come in pairs: 23 inherited from the mother and 23 from the father. The two members of a pair carry the same genes, the stretches of DNA that each affect a particular trait, in the same order, though they may carry different versions of those genes, and they are called **homologous chromosomes**. A cell with two sets in this way is **diploid**.
Chromosome numbers are written with n for the number in a single set, so a diploid cell has 2n chromosomes.

afterFigure.text: Counting the pairs and doubling gives the number of chromosomes in the cell.

lead.text: The sex cells, the egg and the sperm, are called **gametes**, and each carries only one chromosome from each pair of [[homologous chromosomes|The two matching chromosomes of a pair, one from each parent. Met earlier in this lesson.]], which is a single set. A cell with one set is **haploid**, with n chromosomes. When a sperm and an egg fuse in **fertilisation**, their two sets are brought together and the first cell of the new individual is diploid again.

This was established in stages. In 1876 Oscar Hertwig watched under the microscope as a sea urchin sperm entered an egg and the two nuclei fused, and in 1883 Edouard van Beneden found that the gametes of the roundworm *Ascaris* carry half as many chromosomes as its body cells do. If gametes were diploid, the number would double in every generation.

afterFigure.text: **A gamete has half the chromosomes of the cell that made it, one from each pair**, and a haploid number is always half the diploid one.

lead.text: The division that makes gametes is called **meiosis**. As in mitosis, the DNA is copied first, so that every chromosome consists of two sister chromatids, and then two divisions follow without further copying. In the first, **meiosis I**, the homologous chromosomes pair up and the two members of each pair are pulled to opposite ends of the cell, each still made of its two chromatids. This is the step that *halves* the chromosome number, and it gives two cells, each with one chromosome from every pair.

afterFigure.text: The first case of the figure shows a cell with three pairs after copying, with 6 chromosomes and 12 DNA molecules. The second case shows the first division complete, with two cells that have 3 chromosomes each, still copied, so each holds 6 DNA molecules.

lead.text: The second division, **meiosis II**, is much like mitosis. The sister chromatids of each chromosome are pulled apart, and each of the two cells from meiosis I divides, so that **one cell makes four**. Every one of the four has one chromosome of each pair, each now a single chromatid, which makes the cell haploid and ready for fertilisation.

afterFigure.text: The two divisions together reduce the number from 6 chromosomes in the starting cell to 3 in each gamete, and the whole reduction happens in meiosis I, because meiosis II only separates chromatids.

steps.headline: Why no two gametes are alike

lead.text: The four cells from one meiosis are not identical to each other or to their parent. In meiosis I, each homologous pair lines up independently of the others, so which member of a pair goes to which end is decided by chance for every pair. This is **independent assortment**. With two pairs there are 4 possible combinations in a gamete, with three pairs 8, and with 23 pairs 2 multiplied by itself 23 times, which is 8,388,608.

A second shuffle comes earlier in meiosis I, when homologous chromosomes lie side by side and swap matching segments, a step called **crossing over**, which produces chromosomes that are a mixture of the two parents' versions. Then fertilisation adds more variety, because any sperm may meet any egg. Ignoring crossing over, two parents could make 2^23 × 2^23, or about 70 trillion, different combinations, which is why brothers and sisters, except identical twins, differ.

lessons.orientation: How meiosis halves the chromosome number to make gametes through two divisions, and how it shuffles chromosomes to make every gamete different.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: For about thirty years after Theophilus Painter reported in 1923 that human cells contain 48 chromosomes, textbooks repeated the figure, until in 1956 Joe Hin Tjio and Albert Levan, using a new way of spreading the chromosomes of cultured cells flat under the microscope, counted *46* and could not make it 48.

The number raises a question about eggs and sperm. An egg and a sperm fuse to make the first cell of a new person, and that cell has 46 chromosomes, like nearly every other cell in the body, yet the count stays at 46 from one generation to the next. The kind of division that makes egg and sperm cells, **meiosis**, is what keeps it there.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to count chromosomes in diploid and haploid cells and follow the two divisions of meiosis.
intro.whyItMatters: Meiosis keeps the chromosome number steady from one generation to the next, and its shuffling is why offspring differ from their parents.

recap.keyIdea: Meiosis halves the chromosome number in two divisions to make haploid gametes, and fertilisation restores the diploid number.

blocks.text: A **diploid** cell holds pairs of homologous chromosomes, and **meiosis** copies its DNA once and divides twice: meiosis I pulls the homologous chromosomes apart, and meiosis II pulls apart the [[sister chromatids|The two identical, joined copies of a replicated chromosome. Met in 'Copy a message one base at a time'.]]. One cell becomes four **haploid** gametes, each with one chromosome from every pair.
Independent assortment and crossing over make the gametes different from one another, and fertilisation combines two of them, so that each child has a new set of chromosomes.

recap.nextHook: Each chromosome in a pair can carry a different version of a gene, and the next lesson uses a simple cross to predict which versions the offspring inherit.

lessons.title: What could the offspring inherit?

lead.text: A gene is a stretch of DNA that affects a particular trait, such as the shape of a pea. Because chromosomes come in pairs, an individual has two copies of each gene, one from each parent, and the two copies may be different versions, called **alleles**. Mendel's "factors" were what we now call alleles, and the words gene and genotype were coined by Wilhelm Johannsen in 1909.

Alleles are written as letters, a capital for one allele and the matching small letter for the other, so a plant may carry A and a. The pair of alleles an individual carries is its **genotype**. A genotype with two of the same allele, AA or aa, is **homozygous**, and one with two different alleles, Aa, is **heterozygous**.

Each gamete takes one chromosome of every pair, as the lesson on meiosis showed, so it takes one allele of each gene. An AA parent can pass on only A, an aa parent only a, and an Aa parent passes on A or a with *equal* chance.

To predict the [[genotypes|The pair of alleles an individual carries, such as AA or Aa. Met earlier in this lesson.]] of the offspring, write one parent's two possible gametes along the top of a grid and the other parent's down the side, so that each of the four boxes holds one combination. The grid is named for Reginald Punnett, who used it in the early 1900s, and **each box is one equally likely pairing**, because each parent is equally likely to pass on either of its alleles.

Take a cross of AA with Aa. The AA parent can pass on only A, and the Aa parent passes on A or a, so the four boxes read AA, Aa, AA and Aa, which means half of the offspring are expected to be AA and half Aa. The second case of the figure crosses AA with aa, in which every box reads Aa.

afterFigure.text: Move the slider under the figure to inspect one box at a time. The square tells you the genotypes that are *possible* and how likely each one is. It does not say which one any particular offspring will receive.

lead.text: The trait you can observe, such as round or wrinkled seeds, is the **phenotype**, a word that Johannsen coined at the same time as genotype. It depends on the genotype, but not in a one-to-one way. In Mendel's peas a plant with Aa has round seeds, just like a plant with AA, because the allele for round hides the other, and an allele that behaves like this is **dominant** while the one that is hidden is **recessive**. The recessive trait shows *only* in a plant with no dominant allele, which here means aa.

This means that the phenotype does not reveal the genotype. A plant with the dominant trait may be AA or Aa, and the two look identical. A **test cross** tells them apart: breed the plant with an aa plant, and if the plant is Aa, some of the offspring will be aa and show the recessive trait, while the offspring of an AA plant never will.

afterFigure.text: The first case of the figure shows that AA crossed with Aa gives offspring that are all AA or Aa, so every one of them shows the dominant trait. The second, AA crossed with aa, gives all Aa, which again shows the dominant trait, even though none of those offspring is homozygous.

lead.text: A test cross breeds a plant of unknown genotype with an aa plant.

A percentage from a [[Punnett square|A grid that lists every equally likely pairing of two parents' gametes. Met earlier in this lesson.]] is a **probability**, the chance that one particular offspring has that genotype. Each fertilisation is a new draw, so what happened to one offspring has no effect on the next, in the way that a coin that has landed heads three times is still equally likely to land heads or tails.
A ratio therefore appears only over many offspring. A litter of four, or a pod of four seeds, can have any mixture.

afterFigure.text: Each offspring has the same chance of each genotype whatever its brothers and sisters received, so four offspring do not have to split neatly among the boxes.

lessons.orientation: How alleles pass from parents to offspring in a single-gene cross, and how to separate the genotype, the phenotype and the probability.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: In 1866 an Augustinian friar, Gregor Mendel, published the results of eight years of crossing pea plants in the garden of his monastery in Brno. When he crossed plants with round seeds and plants with wrinkled seeds, every plant of the next generation had round seeds, yet when those plants bred among themselves the wrinkled seeds *came back*, 1,850 of them among 7,324 seeds counted.

The numbers were too regular to be chance, and Mendel proposed that each plant carries two "factors" for each trait, one from each parent. His factors are what are now called genes, and his rule lets you predict from the traits of two parents the chances for each trait in their offspring. For a single gene the rule can be drawn as a table, and three things are easily confused and must be kept apart: **the genes an organism carries, the trait that shows, and the chance that decides which genes an offspring receives**.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to work out the chances of an offspring's genotype and phenotype from a single-gene cross.
intro.whyItMatters: The same square predicts the chances of inheriting traits in plants, animals and families, as long as one gene decides the trait.

recap.keyIdea: Each parent passes on one allele, a Punnett square lists the equally likely pairings, and a dominant allele can hide a recessive one in the phenotype.

blocks.text: Each parent passes on one [[allele|One version of a gene. Met earlier in this lesson.]], so a **Punnett square** lists the four equally likely pairings and gives the *probability* of each genotype in an offspring. The phenotype follows from the genotype through dominance, so a dominant allele shows its trait in both AA and Aa, and the recessive trait appears only in aa.
The percentages describe the chance for each offspring and do not guarantee the mix in any one family, which only shows up over many offspring.

recap.nextHook: Alleles themselves come from changes in DNA, and the next lesson asks where a new variant comes from in the first place.

lessons.title: Where does a new variant come from?

lead.text: DNA is copied with great accuracy, because the enzyme that builds the new strand checks each base as it goes and repair systems correct most of the mistakes that remain. Some changes still get through, and others are caused by radiation or chemicals. A change in the sequence of bases in DNA is called a **mutation**.

The simplest kind is a **substitution**, in which one base is replaced by another and the length of the sequence stays the same. In an **insertion** an extra base is added and in a **deletion** one is lost, and either of these changes the length.

afterFigure.text: The first case of the figure shows a short stretch of DNA and the second shows the same stretch after one substitution, with a C replaced by a G.

lead.text: To find a mutation, line up the original and the changed sequence so that each position sits above its partner, and **compare them one position at a time**. Every position where the two letters differ is one change. The sequences TTGCA and TTGGA, for example, agree at positions 1, 2, 3 and 5 and differ only at position 4, where C has become G.

This method works only when the sequences are the *same length*, which is the case for substitutions. An insertion or a deletion shifts everything after it, so the two sequences must be lined up again around the change before the positions can be compared.

A mutation is copied each time its cell divides, so it is passed to all that cell's descendants. If it arises in a skin cell, it stays in the skin cells that descend from that one, and no child can inherit it, because children grow from the egg and sperm and not from the skin.

A mutation that arises in the cells that make **gametes**, or in a gamete itself, can be passed on. If that gamete takes part in fertilisation, the mutation is present in the first cell of the child, and so in every cell that descends from it. **Only mutations in gametes are inherited**, and they are the source of new alleles in a population.

A mutation is not a response to need. In 1943 Salvador Luria and Max Delbrück grew many separate cultures of bacteria and then exposed each to a virus that kills them. The numbers of resistant bacteria varied enormously from one culture to another, with a few cultures holding many and most holding none. That pattern fits resistance [[mutations|Changes in the order of bases in DNA. Met earlier in this lesson.]] that arose by chance at random times *before* the virus was added, and it does not fit resistance that appears because the virus is there, which would give similar numbers in every culture.

Mutation therefore supplies new variants, and **a separate process decides which ones spread**. If a variant helps its carriers survive and reproduce in their environment, it becomes more common in later generations, and if it does not, it stays rare or disappears.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows the same starting population of 20 blue and 20 gold individuals in both cases, with blue becoming more common in one and gold in the other. In neither case did the organisms make the variants they needed: the variants were present at the start, and the environment changed how many of each were left.

lessons.orientation: How a change in DNA creates a new variant, which changes can be inherited, and why mutations are random with respect to need.
lessons.reviewLabel: Where does a new variant come from?

blocks.text: In 1956 Vernon Ingram showed that the whole difference between normal haemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen in red blood cells, and the haemoglobin of people with sickle cell disease is a single building block in one of its chains, which has 146: a valine where the normal protein has a glutamic acid. One changed building block in a protein of that size is enough to change the shape of the red blood cells that carry it.

The protein is built from instructions in a gene, so the cause lies in the DNA, where a change of **one base** produces that change of one building block. Every new allele in a population begins with a change of this kind, so knowing how such changes arise, and which of them can be passed to a child, explains where inherited variation comes from in the first place.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to identify and count changes in a DNA sequence and say which can be inherited and why they are not made to order.
intro.whyItMatters: Mutation is the original source of every new variant, and natural selection has nothing to act on without it.

recap.keyIdea: A mutation is a change in the order of bases in DNA, only a mutation in a gamete is inherited, and mutations arise by chance and not because they are needed.

blocks.text: A **mutation** may be a substitution, which keeps the length of the sequence, or an insertion or a deletion, which change it, and comparing two aligned sequences position by position counts the changes. Only a mutation in a [[gamete|A sex cell, an egg or a sperm, carrying one set of chromosomes. Met in 'Halve a chromosome set'.]] can be passed to a child.
Mutations arise *by chance* and not because they are needed, and the environment then decides which variants become more common, which is the subject of the next lesson.

recap.nextHook: Mutation supplies the variants, and the next lesson asks how a population changes over generations when some variants leave more offspring than others.

lessons.title: A population changes over generations

lead.text: The **frequency** of a variant is the number of individuals that carry it divided by the total number in the population, usually written as a percentage. Among 40 beetles, 24 of them blue, the frequency of blue is 24 ÷ 40 × 100, which is 60%, and the other 16 are gold.

A frequency says nothing about the numbers themselves, since 60% describes 24 of 40 and 600 of 1,000 *equally* well, so it is the right quantity for comparing populations of different size, or the same population at different times.

The figure follows a population of 40 beetles in which blue begins at 24, a [[frequency|The share of a population that carries a variant, written as a percentage. Met earlier in this lesson.]] of 60%. In the first case the birds find the blue beetles more easily, and the blue count falls to 16 of 40, which is 40%, while in the second they find the gold ones more easily and the blue count rises to 32 of 40, which is 80%.

The change is the later frequency minus the earlier one, and it is stated in **percentage points**. Blue has fallen by 60 − 40 = 20 points in the first case and risen by 80 − 60 = 20 points in the second. Percentage points compare two percentages directly, and they are *not* the same as a percentage change in the number of beetles.

Natural selection follows when three conditions hold. The individuals of a population differ from one another, as the mutations of the last lesson ensure. Some of the differences are **heritable**, which means they pass from parents to offspring through DNA. And individuals with some variants leave more surviving offspring than others in their environment. Then the variants of the more successful individuals make up a larger share of the next generation, and their frequency rises generation after generation. This process is **natural selection**.
The change is in the population. No individual changes its heritable makeup during its life, and the change is not planned: it is what the differences in survival and reproduction add up to.

The peppered moth is the best-known example. Field experiments in the 1950s by Bernard Kettlewell, repeated in the 2000s by Michael Majerus, found that birds ate more of the moths that contrasted with the bark, which is selection at work.
A variant is not good or bad in itself. Whether it helps depends on the environment.

afterFigure.text: The figure starts both populations at 20 blue and 20 gold. In the bluebell wood the blue beetles are the less visible, and blue rises to 28 of 40, which is 70%, while in the golden meadow gold is the less visible and blue falls to 12 of 40, which is 30%. **The direction of the change follows the environment.**

lead.text: In a golden meadow the blue beetles are the easier ones to see.

Selection is *not* the only way a frequency can change. In a small population chance alone can shift it, because the individuals that happen to survive or breed may not be a representative sample, a process called **genetic drift**. A frequency can also change when individuals arrive from another population, which is called **migration**.

Because of this, a change in frequency shows that something happened and not what caused it. To show selection you need evidence that the variants differ in survival or reproduction in that environment, as the bird experiments did for the moths.

afterFigure.text: In the first case of the figure a storm leaves only 4 of 10 individuals alive, and the blue share happens to rise from 50% to 75% with no difference in survival or reproduction between the variants. In the second, gold beetles arrive from elsewhere, and the blue share falls from 50% to 25% although no beetle died.

lessons.orientation: How heritable variation and differences in reproductive success change a population over generations, and why a change in frequency does not prove selection.
