items.label: DNA
items.explanation: A bacterium has no nucleus, but its DNA lies in an open region of the cell.

items.label: Nucleus
items.explanation: A bacterium has none. Its DNA lies in a nucleoid with no membrane around it.

items.label: Mitochondria
items.explanation: A bacterium has none, though it still releases energy from fuel.

items.label: Chloroplasts
items.explanation: Only eukaryotic cells exposed to light, such as leaf cells, have them.

questions.onCorrect: The membrane, DNA and ribosomes are shared by every cell. The nucleus, mitochondria and chloroplasts belong to eukaryotic cells.

questions.prompt: Equal volumes hold 12 solute units on the left and 4 on the right, and solute can cross. In which direction is there net movement at first?
hints: Compare the two sides: with equal volumes, the side holding more units has the higher concentration.
Random movement carries more molecules away from the crowded side than back into it.
Net movement runs from the side with more solute towards the side with less.

acceptedIdeas: From left to right
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: From left to right

choices.label: Neither way, because the solute can cross in both directions
From right to left
From left to right

questions.onCorrect: The left side holds more solute, so more molecules cross away from it than into it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the direction towards the crowded side. Net movement runs away from the side that holds more solute.
Molecules do cross both ways, but with 12 units on the left and 4 on the right more of them cross from the left, so there is a net movement until the sides are equal.

questions.prompt: Two fixed equal volumes contain 10 and 6 units of freely crossing solute. How many units are on each side at equilibrium?
hints: Every unit that leaves one side arrives on the other, so the total stays the same.
Add the two starting amounts together first.
Equal volumes end with equal amounts, so divide the total by two.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The 16 units divide equally: 16 ÷ 2 = 8.

questions.onCorrect: Together the sides hold 16 units, and equal volumes end with equal shares, so each holds 8.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total on both sides together. At equilibrium it is divided between the two sides.
That is the amount the left side started with. Net movement carries some of it across, so the left side changes.
That is the amount the right side started with. It gains solute from the left, so it does not stay at its starting value.

questions.prompt: 12 solute units start on the left of a barrier and 4 on the right. The barrier blocks both solute and water. What happens to the amount of solute on the left over a long time?
hints: Ask first what the barrier lets through.
If nothing crosses, nothing can be shared out between the sides.

acceptedIdeas: It stays at 12 units, because nothing can get across
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It stays at 12 units, because nothing can get across

choices.label: It falls towards 8 units, as the sides even out
It stays at 12 units, because nothing can get across
It falls to 4 units, to match the right side

questions.onCorrect: The barrier blocks everything, so neither side can gain or lose solute and the left side keeps its 12 units.

misconceptions.feedback: That is where the amounts would settle if solute could cross. This barrier blocks it, so there is no sharing.
That would need solute to leave the left side, but this barrier lets none cross.

questions.prompt: Dye is added to the left side of a container whose membrane the dye can cross, with equal volumes on both sides. Put these events in the order they happen.
hints: Start with what is different between the two sides at the beginning.
Net movement stops when the concentrations are equal, but the molecules themselves never stop moving.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The left side starts more concentrated, so more molecules cross to the right than back. The counts move towards each other until the sides are equal, and then the crossings in the two directions balance.

items: All the dye is on the left, so the left side is more concentrated
More dye molecules cross from left to right than from right to left
The count on the left falls and the count on the right rises
The two sides reach the same concentration
Molecules keep crossing both ways at equal rates, with no net movement

questions.onCorrect: The difference drives the net movement, and the movement removes the difference. At equilibrium the crossings balance.

questions.prompt: A student wants to know whether a membrane lets a dye through. She puts all the dye on the left, with equal volumes of water on both sides, and checks the right side after an hour. Which result would show that the dye can cross?
hints: Think about where the dye would be if the membrane let it through.
A result that looks the same whether or not the dye crosses cannot tell the two apart.

acceptedIdeas: Dye is found on the right side as well as on the left
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Dye is found on the right side as well as on the left

choices.label: The dye is still all on the left, and the two sides look the same
The water level on the left is higher than the water level on the right
Dye is found on the right side as well as on the left

questions.onCorrect: Only dye on the right side shows that it crossed. A result that looks the same with or without crossing tests nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: That result fits a membrane that blocks the dye. If the dye could cross, some of it would have reached the right side.
A change in water level shows that water moved. It says nothing about whether the dye crossed.

questions.prompt: Water can cross but solute cannot. Equal volumes hold 4 solute units on the left and 12 on the right, at equal pressure. Which side gains water at first?
hints: Compare the concentrations of solute on the two sides. Equal volumes mean the side with more units is more concentrated.
Only water can cross, so the solute stays where it is.
Water moves towards the side with the higher solute concentration.

acceptedIdeas: The right side, which holds more solute
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The right side, which holds more solute

choices.label: Neither side, because the pressures are equal
The right side, which holds more solute
The left side, which holds less solute

questions.onCorrect: It holds more solute in the same volume, and only water is free to move.

misconceptions.feedback: The left side has the lower solute concentration, so water leaves it. Water moves towards the side with more solute.
Equal pressure means that nothing pushes back at the start, so the difference in solute is free to draw water towards the right.

questions.prompt: A compartment contains 12 solute units in volume 2. What is its concentration in units per volume?
hints: Concentration compares the amount of solute with the space it fills.
Both the amount and the volume are given in the question.
Divide the amount of solute by the volume.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Concentration = 12 ÷ 2 = 6 units per volume.

questions.onCorrect: Concentration is solute divided by volume, so 12 units in a volume of 2 gives 6 units per volume.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the amount of solute, not its concentration. Concentration is the amount divided by the volume it fills.
Multiplying the amount by the volume gives a number with no meaning here. Concentration is the amount divided by the volume.
Adding the amount and the volume mixes two different kinds of quantity. Concentration is the amount divided by the volume.

questions.prompt: A potted plant is left unwatered and wilts. What has happened inside its cells?
hints: A plant that loses water through its leaves loses something that pushed against the cell walls.
Think about which way the water is moving.

acceptedIdeas: They lost water, and with it the pressure that held the walls firm
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They lost water, and with it the pressure that held the walls firm

choices.label: Their walls have dissolved, so the cells can no longer hold their shape
They lost water, and with it the pressure that held the walls firm
They have burst, because too much water flowed in

questions.onCorrect: Turgor pressure comes from water inside the cell pressing on the wall. When water is lost the pressure falls and the plant wilts.

misconceptions.feedback: The wall is a rigid layer and stays in place. The plant wilts because the cells lose water and the pressure on the wall falls.
A plant that is short of water loses it from its cells. Cells burst when too much water enters and nothing pushes back.

questions.prompt: A student says an enzyme speeds up a reaction by giving it extra energy. Which reply is best?
hints: The figure on the previous screen shows what changed: the same product, only faster.
Ask which barrier the enzyme acts on, and whether it adds anything to the reaction.

acceptedIdeas: It lowers the barrier the reaction must cross and supplies no energy
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It lowers the barrier the reaction must cross and supplies no energy

choices.label: It lowers the barrier the reaction must cross and supplies no energy
That is right, because the extra energy is what makes the product form faster
That is wrong, because an enzyme is used up as the reaction runs

questions.onCorrect: An enzyme lowers the activation energy and comes out unchanged, so the only thing it changes is how fast the reaction goes.

misconceptions.feedback: An enzyme supplies no energy. It offers a route with a lower barrier, and the same product forms faster.
An enzyme comes out of the reaction unchanged, so one molecule can work on batch after batch. What is wrong with the claim is the energy.

questions.prompt: In an enzyme reaction every active site is busy, and adding more substrate no longer raises the rate. What limits the rate?
hints: Think about what has run out of free active sites.
Adding substrate has stopped helping, so substrate is not the limit.

acceptedIdeas: The enzyme
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The enzyme

choices.label: The substrate
The temperature
The enzyme

questions.onCorrect: The enzyme. Once every active site is busy, only more enzyme can raise the rate.

misconceptions.feedback: There is already more substrate than the active sites can use, which is why adding more makes no difference.
Temperature can limit a reaction, but nothing in the question suggests it has changed. The question points to what has run out.

questions.prompt: A sample of substrate with enzyme makes 27 units of product in 3 minutes, and the student says the enzyme made all 27. Which extra sample would test that claim?
hints: The claim is that the enzyme made all of the product.
What would the product be if the enzyme were absent and nothing else changed?

acceptedIdeas: A matched sample with no enzyme, to show what forms anyway
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A matched sample with no enzyme, to show what forms anyway

choices.label: A sample with twice as much enzyme, to see whether it makes more
The same sample measured again, to check the 27
A matched sample with no enzyme, to show what forms anyway

questions.onCorrect: A matched sample without the enzyme, the control, shows what forms anyway. Only the extra product can be credited to the enzyme.

misconceptions.feedback: More enzyme tests whether the amount matters. It does not show how much product forms with no enzyme at all.
Measuring the same sample again checks the reading. It cannot show what forms without the enzyme.

questions.prompt: A high-temperature treatment lowers one enzyme's activity. What is a plausible explanation?
hints: Think about what high temperatures do to a folded protein.
Activity depends on the substrate fitting the enzyme's active site, so ask what happens to that fit when the protein loses its shape.

acceptedIdeas: Its active-site shape has changed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: High temperature can denature an enzyme and disrupt binding or catalysis.

choices.label: The enzyme has been used up by the reaction
Heat always increases enzyme activity
Its active-site shape has changed

questions.onCorrect: Its active-site shape has changed. Heat can unfold an enzyme, and the substrate then no longer fits.

misconceptions.feedback: An enzyme comes out of the reaction unchanged, so it is not used up.
Heat speeds an enzyme up only until its shape begins to change. After that it lowers the activity.

questions.prompt: Which experiment best tests an enzyme's effect?
hints: The only difference between the samples should be the thing you are testing.
Repeating the samples shows how much they vary.

acceptedIdeas: Matched samples with and without enzyme, each repeated
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Matched samples with and without enzyme, each repeated

choices.label: Matched samples with and without enzyme, each repeated
One sample with the enzyme, measured several times
Two samples, one with the enzyme and one kept warmer

questions.onCorrect: Matched, replicated samples that differ only in enzyme addition, so any difference can be credited to the enzyme.

misconceptions.feedback: Measuring one sample again shows how much it varies, but with no matched sample lacking the enzyme there is nothing to compare it against.
The samples differ in temperature as well as in the enzyme, so a difference could be due to either.

questions.prompt: A willow shoot grows for five years in a pot, given only water, and gains about 164 pounds while its soil loses about 2 ounces. A student says the new wood was made from the water. Which fact counts against that?
hints: Look at the equation: which input contains carbon?
The soil lost almost nothing, so something else must have supplied the carbon.

acceptedIdeas: Wood is about half carbon, and water has no carbon to supply it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Wood is about half carbon, and water has no carbon to supply it

choices.label: Water is too light to build wood, so the soil must have supplied it
Wood is about half carbon, and water has no carbon to supply it
Light energy is turned into the carbon atoms in the wood

questions.onCorrect: The carbon came from carbon dioxide in the air. Water supplied hydrogen and oxygen, light supplied energy, and the soil supplied almost nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: The soil lost only about 2 ounces, far too little to account for 164 pounds of wood.
Light supplies energy and has no atoms to add. The carbon atoms come from a gas in the air, carbon dioxide.

questions.prompt: One glucose has six carbon atoms. Each CO₂ supplies one. How many CO₂ molecules supply the carbon for five glucose molecules?
hints: Count the carbon atoms in the glucose that is made.
Each glucose has six carbon atoms and each CO₂ brings one.
Multiply the number of glucose molecules by six.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Five glucose contain 5 × 6 = 30 carbon atoms, so they need 30 CO₂.

questions.onCorrect: Five glucose contain 5 × 6 = 30 carbon atoms, and each CO₂ supplies one, so 30 are needed.

misconceptions.feedback: Six CO₂ would supply the carbon for a single glucose. Five glucose need five times as many.
That is the number of glucose molecules. Each one needs six CO₂, since it contains six carbon atoms.
Adding 5 and 6 does not count the carbon. Each of the five glucose needs six CO₂, so multiply.

questions.prompt: A student sees that a leaf takes in light, finds no light among the products in the equation, and concludes that the energy vanished. In what form is the energy actually stored in the glucose?
hints: The energy cannot disappear, so ask where the leaf's product could hold it.
Light has no atoms, so it cannot become carbon or oxygen. Think about what the bonds in glucose can store.

acceptedIdeas: chemical energy
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is stored as chemical energy in the bonds of the glucose.

questions.onCorrect: Chlorophyll absorbs the light, and the energy is stored as chemical energy in the bonds of glucose until a cell needs it.

misconceptions.feedback: Light is the form in which the energy arrives. The question asks for the form in which it is stored.
Some energy does disperse as heat, but what the leaf stores in glucose is a different form.
Energy is not turned into atoms. The question asks for the form in which the glucose holds the energy.

questions.prompt: In photosynthesis, which of these does a leaf take in as matter, which as energy, and which does it make?
hints: Matter has atoms that end up in the products, and energy has none.
The products are what the leaf builds or releases.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Carbon dioxide and water are taken in as matter, light is taken in as energy, and the leaf makes glucose and oxygen.

items.label: Carbon dioxide
items.explanation: Its carbon atoms are built into glucose.

items.label: Water
items.explanation: Its atoms end up in glucose and in the oxygen that is released.

items.label: Light
items.explanation: It has no atoms. Chlorophyll absorbs it and the energy is stored in the glucose.

items.label: Glucose
items.explanation: It is the sugar the leaf builds, with six carbon atoms in each molecule.

items.label: Oxygen
items.explanation: It is released into the air as a product of the process.

questions.onCorrect: Carbon dioxide and water supply the atoms, light supplies the energy, and the leaf builds glucose and releases oxygen.

questions.prompt: A muscle cell uses ATP to do a piece of work. What happens to the ATP afterwards?
hints: ATP carries energy to where work is done and then delivers it.
Ask what is left after it delivers its energy, and whether the cell can restore it.

acceptedIdeas: It loses a phosphate group, and respiration then rebuilds it for reuse
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It loses a phosphate group, and respiration then rebuilds it for reuse

choices.label: It loses a phosphate group, and respiration then rebuilds it for reuse
It is used up, so the cell has to find a new supply from its food
It turns into glucose, which stores the energy for later

questions.onCorrect: ATP loses one phosphate group when it delivers its energy, and respiration adds it back, so the same molecules carry energy again and again.

misconceptions.feedback: ATP is not used up. Respiration rebuilds it, so the same molecules are used again and again.
Glucose is the fuel, and ATP does not turn into it. ATP loses a phosphate group and is rebuilt using energy from the fuel.

questions.prompt: A cell completely breaks down two glucose molecules using oxygen. How many CO₂ molecules does it produce?
hints: Count the carbon atoms in the two glucose molecules.
Each glucose has six carbon atoms, and each CO₂ takes one.
Multiply the number of glucose molecules by six.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each glucose contributes six carbon atoms: 2 × 6 = 12 CO₂.

questions.onCorrect: Two glucose hold 2 × 6 = 12 carbon atoms, and each leaves in its own CO₂, so 12 CO₂ are produced.

misconceptions.feedback: Six CO₂ carry away the carbon of a single glucose. Two glucose give twice as many.
That is the number of glucose molecules. Each one gives six CO₂.
Adding 2 and 6 does not count the carbon. Each of the two glucose gives six CO₂, so multiply.

questions.prompt: A student seals germinating peas in a jar and sees the oxygen fall from 20 units to 11 in three minutes. She says respiration used all 9 units. What should she add to her set-up to test that?
hints: Oxygen can fall for reasons that have nothing to do with the organisms.
A matched set-up without the organisms would show how much of the change happens anyway.

acceptedIdeas: A second jar set up the same way, with no peas in it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A second jar set up the same way, with no peas in it

choices.label: A second jar with twice as many peas, to compare the amounts
A second jar set up the same way, with no peas in it
The same jar, left for longer to see how far it falls

questions.onCorrect: A blank jar with no peas shows how much oxygen is lost anyway, for example through a leak or by gas dissolving in water.

misconceptions.feedback: More peas would test whether the amount matters. It would not show how much oxygen disappears when there are no peas.
Waiting longer shows how the fall continues. It cannot separate the peas' use from other causes.

questions.prompt: What happens to glucose's carbon when a cell breaks the glucose down completely using oxygen?
hints: Atoms are rearranged and never lost.
Think about where the carbon of the fuel goes in the equation.

acceptedIdeas: It appears in carbon dioxide
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Glucose carbon is conserved in CO₂; energy transfer does not destroy those atoms.

choices.label: It is carried away in the water that is made
It vanishes as energy
It appears in carbon dioxide

questions.onCorrect: It appears in carbon dioxide. Energy is released, but the carbon atoms are only rearranged.

misconceptions.feedback: Atoms are never turned into energy in these reactions. The carbon atoms are rearranged into another molecule.
Water contains hydrogen and oxygen but no carbon. The carbon leaves in a different product.

questions.prompt: Which claim correctly separates breathing from cellular respiration?
hints: One of these moves air and the other happens inside cells.
Think about which one releases energy from fuel.

acceptedIdeas: Breathing moves air, and respiration releases energy from fuel
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Breathing moves air, and respiration releases energy from fuel

choices.label: They are one process, and both happen in the lungs
Breathing releases energy from fuel, and respiration moves air
Breathing moves air, and respiration releases energy from fuel

questions.onCorrect: Breathing moves air in and out, and cellular respiration is the chemical reactions in cells that transfer energy from fuel.

misconceptions.feedback: Breathing is the movement of air into and out of the lungs. Respiration is a set of chemical reactions that goes on in every living cell.
That swaps the two. Ask which of them is a movement of air and which is a set of chemical reactions in cells.

questions.prompt: A sample of double-stranded DNA is 30% adenine. What percentage of its bases is guanine?
hints: Every A is paired with a T, so the sample holds as much T as A.
Work out how much is left for C and G, and remember that they pair with each other.
Share what is left between C and G equally.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A pairs with T, so T is also 30%. A and T make 60%, which leaves 40% for C and G. They pair with each other, so each is 20%.

questions.onCorrect: Adenine pairs with thymine, so A and T are each 30% and C and G share the other 40%, with 20% each.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the percentage of adenine. Thymine is also 30%, and guanine belongs to the other pair.
That is the share of cytosine and guanine together. Each of them is half of it.
That is adenine and thymine together. Guanine is in the other pair.

questions.prompt: Which strand, written left to right, is the partner of the strand 5′-AAGC-3′?
hints: Pair each base in turn, from the left.
The pairs are A with T and C with G.
The first two bases are both A, so the first two partners are alike.

acceptedIdeas: TTCG
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: TTCG

choices.label: GCTT
TTGC
CCTG
TTCG

questions.onCorrect: TTCG. A takes T, G takes C and C takes G, base by base.

misconceptions.feedback: Those are the right partners in reverse order. Write the partners from left to right, in the same order as the strand.
The A bases are paired correctly, but G and C have been left as they were. G pairs with C and C pairs with G.
That pairs A with C and G with T. The pairs are A with T and C with G.

questions.prompt: A cell has 4 chromosomes before its DNA is copied. Right after copying, with the sister chromatids still joined, what does it hold?
hints: Think about what is counted as one chromosome after copying.
The two sister chromatids stay joined and count together.
Each chromatid holds one DNA molecule.

acceptedIdeas: 4 chromosomes and 8 DNA molecules
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 4 chromosomes and 8 DNA molecules

choices.label: 4 chromosomes and 8 DNA molecules
8 chromosomes and 8 DNA molecules
4 chromosomes and 4 DNA molecules

questions.onCorrect: Four chromosomes with 8 DNA molecules. Copying doubles the DNA molecules, but joined sister chromatids still count as one chromosome.

misconceptions.feedback: Joined sister chromatids are counted as one chromosome, so copying adds DNA molecules and not chromosomes.
Each chromosome now holds two DNA molecules, one in each chromatid, so the molecules have doubled.

questions.prompt: Put the steps by which a cell copies one DNA molecule in order.
hints: The strands have to be apart before either one can act as a template.
The bases are matched before an enzyme joins them, and the finished molecules come last.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Enzymes unwind and separate the strands, each old strand then serves as a template, free bases are matched to it one at a time, polymerase joins them into a new strand, and two molecules result that each keep one old strand.

items: Enzymes unwind the double helix and separate its two strands
Each old strand serves as a template
Free bases are matched to the template one at a time, A to T and C to G
DNA polymerase joins the matched bases into a new strand
Two molecules result, each with one old strand and one new strand

questions.onCorrect: Copying separates the strands first, builds a partner against each one, and ends with two molecules that each keep one old strand.

questions.prompt: A human skin cell with 46 chromosomes divides by mitosis. How many DNA molecules does each daughter cell hold just after the division?
hints: Before the division the cell holds 92 DNA molecules in 46 chromosomes, each made of two sister chromatids.
The two chromatids of every chromosome are pulled to opposite ends.

acceptedIdeas: 46, one in each chromosome
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 46, one in each chromosome

choices.label: 92, because the DNA was copied before the division
46, one in each chromosome
23, because each daughter gets half of the chromosomes

questions.onCorrect: Each daughter receives one chromatid of every chromosome, which is 46 chromosomes with one DNA molecule each. Copying doubles the DNA count and division halves it.

misconceptions.feedback: The 92 molecules are shared out, one chromatid of every chromosome to each daughter, so each daughter holds 46.
Mitosis gives each daughter a complete set of 46 chromosomes. Meiosis is the division that halves the number.

questions.prompt: A cell starts with 4 chromosomes and completes normal mitosis and cytokinesis. What does each daughter cell receive?
hints: Ask what mitosis does to the number of chromosomes.
The chromatids of each chromosome are pulled apart and shared out equally.
Count how many chromatids of each chromosome a daughter cell receives.

acceptedIdeas: A complete set of 4 chromosomes
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A complete set of 4 chromosomes

choices.label: Half of the set, which is 2 chromosomes
A complete set of 4 chromosomes
A set of 8 chromosomes, one for each chromatid

questions.onCorrect: A complete set of 4. Mitosis gives each daughter cell a full set, so the chromosome number is unchanged.

misconceptions.feedback: Mitosis does not halve the chromosome number. Ask what happens to the two chromatids of every chromosome.
Eight is the number of chromatids just before division. Each daughter receives only one chromatid of every chromosome.

questions.prompt: A student counts the cells in a growing culture each hour and gets 100, 200, 400 and 800. What does this pattern suggest?
hints: Look at how each count compares with the one before it.
Adding the same number each hour would give a different pattern.

acceptedIdeas: Every cell is dividing about once an hour, so the number doubles
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Every cell is dividing about once an hour, so the number doubles

choices.label: 100 new cells appear each hour, whatever the number of cells
Only the first cells divide, and the new cells never do
Every cell is dividing about once an hour, so the number doubles

questions.onCorrect: A count that doubles at each step means every cell, new ones included, divides in each round, so the cells grow by multiplying.

misconceptions.feedback: A fixed addition would give 100, 200, 300 and 400. These counts double, which means every cell is dividing.
If only the first 100 cells divided, the count would stop at 200. These counts double every hour, so the new cells divide too.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes what the spindle does in mitosis?
hints: Mitosis starts after the DNA has been copied.
Think about which two things are pulled apart, and where they end up.

acceptedIdeas: It pulls the two sister chromatids of every chromosome to opposite ends
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It pulls the two sister chromatids of every chromosome to opposite ends

choices.label: It pulls the members of each homologous pair into different cells
It pulls the two sister chromatids of every chromosome to opposite ends
It copies each chromosome so that both ends of the cell receive a set

questions.onCorrect: The spindle separates the sister chromatids, so both ends of the cell receive a complete set of chromosomes.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what happens in meiosis I. In mitosis the spindle separates the two chromatids of each chromosome.
The DNA is copied earlier, in interphase. The spindle only shares out the copies that already exist.

questions.prompt: A cell has 6 chromosomes, and each one has a partner that carries the same genes in the same order. How many sets of chromosomes does the cell hold?
hints: Each homologous pair has one chromosome from the mother and one from the father.
Count the pairs, then ask how many sets they make.

acceptedIdeas: Two sets of three chromosomes, so it is diploid
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Two sets of three chromosomes, so it is diploid

choices.label: Two sets of three chromosomes, so it is diploid
One set of six chromosomes, since all six are different
Three sets of two chromosomes, one set for each pair

questions.onCorrect: Three pairs mean two sets of three chromosomes, one set from each parent, so the cell is diploid with 2n = 6.

misconceptions.feedback: Chromosomes that carry the same genes in the same order are homologous partners. Six chromosomes in three such pairs make two sets of three.
Each pair holds one chromosome from each of the two sets. Three pairs mean two sets of three chromosomes, not three sets.

questions.prompt: A student says the chromosome number is halved in the second division of meiosis, when the sister chromatids are pulled apart. In which division is it actually halved?
hints: After the first division each cell has one chromosome from every pair.
The second division works like mitosis, which keeps the chromosome number.

acceptedIdeas: meiosis i
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Meiosis I, when the members of each homologous pair go to different cells.

questions.onCorrect: Meiosis I separates the homologous chromosomes and halves the number. The second division only separates sister chromatids.

misconceptions.feedback: Pulling sister chromatids apart gives each cell single-chromatid chromosomes but leaves the number in each cell as it was. The halving comes earlier.
Fertilisation joins two sets and doubles the number. The halving happens during meiosis.

questions.prompt: A cell has 4 pairs of chromosomes. It copies its DNA and completes meiosis I. What does each of the two new cells hold?
hints: Meiosis I pulls the two members of each pair into different cells.
The sister chromatids stay joined through the first division.

acceptedIdeas: 4 chromosomes, each still made of two chromatids
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 4 chromosomes, each still made of two chromatids

choices.label: 8 chromosomes in each cell, each made of one chromatid
4 chromosomes, each still made of two chromatids
4 chromosomes in each cell, each made of one chromatid

questions.onCorrect: Each cell has one chromosome from every pair, still copied, so it holds 4 chromosomes made of two chromatids each.

misconceptions.feedback: Meiosis I separates whole chromosomes, so the number in each cell halves from 8 to 4. The chromatids stay joined until meiosis II.
The sister chromatids are not pulled apart until meiosis II, so each chromosome is still made of two.

questions.prompt: An Aa plant makes a great many gametes. What mixture of gametes does it make?
hints: Each gamete takes one allele of the gene.
An Aa parent passes on either allele with equal chance.

acceptedIdeas: Half carry A and half carry a
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Half carry A and half carry a

choices.label: All carry A, because A is the dominant allele
Half carry A and half carry a
All carry both A and a, because the plant has both alleles

questions.onCorrect: Each gamete receives one allele, A or a, and an Aa plant passes on each with equal chance.

misconceptions.feedback: Dominance decides which trait shows and has no effect on which allele goes into a gamete. An Aa plant passes on A or a with equal chance.
Each gamete takes one allele of the gene, so it carries A or a.

questions.prompt: For Aa × Aa, what percentage of offspring is expected to have genotype aa?
hints: Draw the four boxes of the square, with the two parents' gametes along its edges.
Each box is one equally likely pairing.
Count the boxes that read aa, and divide by four.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One of four equally likely pairings is aa: 1 ÷ 4 = 25%.

questions.onCorrect: Each parent passes on a with probability one half, so one of the four boxes is aa, which is 1 ÷ 4 = 25%.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the share of offspring that carry at least one A. The question asks only for aa, which needs a from both parents.
That is the share of Aa offspring, which receive a from just one parent. The aa genotype needs a from both.
Each offspring has a chance of receiving a from each parent, not a certainty. Count the aa boxes in the square.

questions.prompt: Four offspring are produced from Aa × Aa. Which statement is justified?
hints: Each seed is a separate fertilisation.
The result for one seed does not change the chance for the next.

acceptedIdeas: Each of the four has a 25% chance of being aa
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each of the four has a 25% chance of being aa

choices.label: Each of the four has a 25% chance of being aa
Exactly one of the four will be aa
The fourth must be aa if the first three are not

questions.onCorrect: Each offspring has a 25% chance of being aa. Chance applies to each one separately and does not promise a family ratio.

misconceptions.feedback: A chance of 25% says how likely each seed is to be aa. It does not guarantee that any set of four contains exactly one.
Each seed is a separate fertilisation, so what happened to the earlier seeds does not change the chance for the next.

questions.prompt: A plant with the dominant trait is crossed with an aa plant. Of 20 offspring, 11 show the dominant trait and 9 show the recessive trait. What is the genotype of the plant with the dominant trait?
hints: An aa plant can pass on only a.
An offspring that shows the recessive trait must have received a from both parents.

acceptedIdeas: Aa, since about half of the offspring show the recessive trait
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Aa, since about half of the offspring show the recessive trait

choices.label: AA, since it shows the dominant trait, and AA is the dominant genotype
aa, since only an aa plant can have offspring with the recessive trait
Aa, since about half of the offspring show the recessive trait

questions.onCorrect: The 9 recessive offspring each received a from this plant, so it carries a. With both A and a it is Aa, which gives a ratio near 1:1.

misconceptions.feedback: An AA plant could pass on only A, so every offspring would show the dominant trait. Recessive offspring show that the plant also carries a.
An aa plant shows the recessive trait, and this plant shows the dominant one, so it carries at least one A.

questions.prompt: Each statement describes a pea plant. Does it describe the plant's genotype or its phenotype?
hints: The genotype is the pair of alleles, and the phenotype is the trait you can observe.
Ask whether you could tell from the statement just by looking at the plant.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Carrying the alleles A and a, having both alleles a and being homozygous describe the genotype. Wrinkled seeds, showing the dominant trait and looking identical describe the phenotype.

items.label: The plant carries the alleles A and a
items.explanation: The pair of alleles an individual carries is its genotype.

items.label: The seeds are wrinkled
items.explanation: Wrinkled seeds are a trait that can be observed.

items.label: Both of the plant's alleles are a
items.explanation: The alleles it carries are the genotype, here aa.

items.label: The plant shows the dominant trait
items.explanation: A trait that can be seen is the phenotype.

items.label: The plant is homozygous
items.explanation: Homozygous describes the two alleles the plant carries.

items.label: Two plants look identical
items.explanation: They share a phenotype, though one may be AA and the other Aa.

questions.onCorrect: Alleles are the genotype and the visible trait is the phenotype, which is why two plants can look the same and carry different alleles.

questions.prompt: In sickle cell disease one base of a gene is changed, and one of the 146 building blocks of a protein changes with it. What does this show?
hints: A substitution swaps one base for another.
Look at how many building blocks changed, out of how many.

acceptedIdeas: One changed base can be enough to change a protein and its cells
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: One changed base can be enough to change a protein and its cells

choices.label: One changed base can be enough to change a protein and its cells
A mutation matters only if it changes many bases at once
A substitution changes the length of the gene, and so the whole protein

questions.onCorrect: One changed base gave one changed building block, which was enough to alter the shape of red blood cells.

misconceptions.feedback: Here a change of one base was enough to change one building block and the shape of the red blood cells that carry it.
A substitution replaces one base with another and keeps the length. Only one building block of the 146 changed.

questions.prompt: The same stretch of a gene reads ACGTAC in a mother, ACGTAC in a father and ACGAAC in their child. Which explanation fits?
hints: Compare the three sequences one position at a time.
Ask which cells could carry a change into a child.

acceptedIdeas: A mutation probably arose in a gamete, so neither parent has the change
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A mutation probably arose in a gamete, so neither parent has the change

choices.label: The child inherited the change from the mother, whose DNA must carry it
A mutation probably arose in a gamete, so neither parent has the change
It is a reading mistake, since a child's DNA must match its parents' DNA

questions.onCorrect: Position 4 reads T in both parents and A in the child. A mutation in a parent's egg or sperm cell can give a child a change that neither parent has.

misconceptions.feedback: The mother's sequence is ACGTAC, the same as the father's. Neither parent carries the change.
A child's DNA is not a copy of either parent's. A mutation in a gamete can give the child a base that neither parent has.

questions.prompt: A mutation arises in one of a parent's skin cells. What is the likely result for the parent's children?
hints: Think about which cells pass DNA to children.
A skin cell is a body cell.

acceptedIdeas: They do not inherit it, because it is not in a gamete
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They do not inherit it, because it is not in a gamete

choices.label: They inherit it, because it is in the parent's DNA
They do not inherit it, because it is not in a gamete
They inherit it only if it harms the parent's skin

questions.onCorrect: A mutation in a body cell stays in that cell and its descendants. Only a mutation in a gamete can reach a child.

misconceptions.feedback: A mutation in a skin cell stays in that cell and its descendants. It is not in the eggs or sperm that make a child.
Whether a mutation is harmful makes no difference to whether it reaches children. Only a mutation in a gamete can.

questions.prompt: 10 of 40 organisms carry the blue variant. What percentage is blue?
hints: Frequency compares the number with the variant to the whole population.
Divide the number of blue organisms by the total, then convert to a percentage.
Multiply the result by 100.
questions.onCorrect: The blue organisms are 10 out of 40, and 10 ÷ 40 × 100 = 25%.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of blue organisms. The frequency is a share of the whole population, written as a percentage.
That counts the organisms that are not blue, 30 of the 40. The question asks for the blue share.
That divides the total by the blue number. The frequency is the blue number divided by the total, times 100.

questions.prompt: Fur colour in a mouse population is inherited. On dark soil owls catch more pale mice, so dark mice leave more young. What happens to the share of dark mice over many generations?
hints: Ask which mice leave more young, and whether their colour is passed on.
Selection changes the share of each variant in the population and does not change the individuals.

acceptedIdeas: It rises, because dark mice leave more young that inherit their colour
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It rises, because dark mice leave more young that inherit their colour

choices.label: It stays the same, because no individual mouse changes colour
It rises, because dark mice leave more young that inherit their colour
It rises, because pale mice turn dark on dark soil

questions.onCorrect: Heritable variants that leave more offspring become more common. No mouse changes colour, and the share of dark ones rises over the generations.

misconceptions.feedback: No mouse changes colour, but the share of dark mice does, because dark mice leave more offspring that inherit the colour.
Mice do not change colour to match the soil. The share rises because dark mice leave more young.

questions.prompt: Blue organisms increase from 15 of 50 to 30 of 50. By how many percentage points does the blue frequency rise?
hints: Work out the blue frequency before and after.
Each is a number out of 50.
Subtract the earlier percentage from the later one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The frequency rises from 30% to 60%, a 30-point increase.

questions.onCorrect: The blue frequency rises from 30% to 60%, which is an increase of 30 percentage points.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the increase in the number of organisms. The question asks about the change in the percentage.
That is the percentage change in the number of blue organisms. The question asks for the difference between the two frequencies, in percentage points.
That is the frequency after the change. The question asks how far it rose from the earlier one.

questions.prompt: A once-useful trait becomes disadvantageous after a habitat change. Is this compatible with natural selection?
hints: Think about what an advantage depends on.
A change of habitat changes which variants do well.

acceptedIdeas: Yes, whether a trait helps depends on the environment
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes, whether a trait helps depends on the environment

choices.label: Yes, whether a trait helps depends on the environment
No, a trait that was useful stays useful in every habitat
Only if the organisms choose to change their traits

questions.onCorrect: Reproductive advantage depends on the environment, so a trait that helped in one habitat can hinder in another.

misconceptions.feedback: A trait is useful or not depending on the environment. When the habitat changes, the advantage can change with it.
Organisms do not choose their heritable traits. Selection acts on differences in reproductive success.

questions.prompt: Each case below is invented. Is the change in the population caused by selection, drift or migration?
hints: Selection needs a consistent difference in survival or reproduction, drift is chance, and migration is arrival from elsewhere.
Ask whether the individuals lost or gained were chosen by a heritable trait.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The beetle and thick-fur cases are selection, the storm and the landslide are drift, and the gold beetles and the wind-blown seeds are migration.

items.label: Birds find blue beetles more easily on golden grass, and the share of blue falls over the generations
items.explanation: Blue beetles survive and breed less, so a difference in survival drives the change.

items.label: A storm kills 6 of 10 mice at random, and by chance the survivors include more brown ones
items.explanation: The survivors were not chosen by colour. Chance in a small group changed the share.

items.label: Gold beetles arrive from another meadow, and the share of blue falls although no beetle died
items.explanation: Individuals arriving from another population changed the share.

items.label: Mice with thicker fur leave more surviving young in a cold winter, and thick fur is inherited
items.explanation: A heritable difference in survival raises the share of thick-furred mice.

items.label: A landslide buries a random handful of snails, and the share of striped shells changes
items.explanation: Chance decided which snails were lost, whatever their shell pattern.

items.label: Wind blows seeds of pale-flowered plants into a meadow of dark-flowered plants
items.explanation: New individuals arrived from elsewhere and added to the population.

questions.onCorrect: Selection follows a heritable difference in survival or reproduction, drift follows chance in who survives, and migration follows arrivals from outside.

questions.prompt: A pond web has algae, zooplankton, small fish and a heron. Which of these is the producer?
hints: A producer builds its own food from light.
A producer does not eat other organisms.

acceptedIdeas: Algae
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Algae

choices.label: The heron
Small fish
Zooplankton
Algae

questions.onCorrect: Algae. They make their own food by photosynthesis, so every route through the pond starts with them.

misconceptions.feedback: A heron eats other animals, so it is a consumer. A producer makes its own food from light.
Small fish eat other organisms, so they are consumers. A producer makes its own food from light.
Zooplankton eat other organisms, so they are consumers. A producer makes its own food from light.

questions.prompt: In a meadow web a hawk eats mice and frogs, frogs eat grasshoppers, and mice and grasshoppers eat grass. If you follow every route back, where does the energy in the hawk come from?
hints: Follow each arrow backwards from the hawk, one step at a time.
Every chain traced back ends at a producer.

acceptedIdeas: From the grass, along two different routes
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: From the grass, along two different routes

choices.label: From the mice and frogs, which are its only food
From the grasshoppers, since they feed the frogs
From the grass, along two different routes

questions.onCorrect: Both routes, grass to mouse to hawk and grass to grasshopper to frog to hawk, begin at the grass, which is the producer.

misconceptions.feedback: The mice and frogs pass on energy that they took from other organisms. Following the arrows back leads to the grass.
The grasshoppers are one route, through the frogs. The mice are another route, and both start at the grass.

questions.prompt: Heat leaves a food web at every step, and no organism can use it to make food. What keeps the web supplied with energy?
hints: Energy flows through an ecosystem in one direction.
Only producers bring energy into the web from outside.

acceptedIdeas: A continuing supply of light for the producers
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A continuing supply of light for the producers

choices.label: A continuing supply of light for the producers
Decomposers, which turn the heat back into food
The nutrients that cycle back through the soil, which carry the energy with them

questions.onCorrect: Energy flows through a web and leaves as heat, so producers have to be supplied again by light, while matter goes round.

misconceptions.feedback: Decomposers return matter, such as nutrients, to the soil and water. They cannot turn heat back into food.
Matter goes round, but the energy does not. The nutrients return atoms, and the energy has to arrive again as light.

questions.prompt: In a meadow food web a hawk eats both mice and frogs. The number of mice goes down. Which prediction does the web support?
hints: A web shows which organisms eat which, not how many.
Other foods and conditions can matter as well.

acceptedIdeas: The hawks may fall, but the web cannot say by how much
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The hawks may fall, but the web cannot say by how much

choices.label: The hawks will fall by exactly as many as the mice did
The hawks cannot be affected, because they also eat frogs
The hawks may fall, but the web cannot say by how much

questions.onCorrect: The arrows show who eats whom and not by how much, and the hawk's other foods and conditions also affect it.

misconceptions.feedback: Arrows show that a feeding link exists. They carry no information about amounts, so no exact number follows.
An organism with another food may be affected less, but losing one food source can still reduce its numbers.

questions.prompt: Energy flows through an ecosystem, while matter goes round. Which of these goes round and is used again, and which flows through?
hints: Matter is atoms, and atoms can be used again. Energy leaves as heat.
Decomposers return matter to the soil and water.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The nitrogen, the carbon atoms and the atoms in the waste go round. The heat, the captured light and the energy in the frog's meal flow through.

bins.label: Goes round and is used again
Flows through and is not used again

items.label: Nitrogen in a dead fish, released by bacteria and taken up by algae
items.explanation: Decomposers return the atoms to the water, where producers build them into new tissue.

items.label: Heat given off by a heron as it hunts
items.explanation: Heat cannot be used by organisms to make food.

items.label: Carbon atoms in a dead leaf that a plant later builds into new tissue
items.explanation: Atoms are never lost, so they can be used again.

items.label: Light captured by algae and passed along the arrows as the energy of food
items.explanation: It enters from outside, passes along the web and leaves as heat.

items.label: Atoms in a fox's waste that fungi return to the soil
items.explanation: Decomposers return nutrients so that producers can take them up.

items.label: The energy in the grasshoppers that a frog eats
items.explanation: It passes along the arrows, and much of it leaves as heat.

questions.onCorrect: Atoms are recycled by decomposers and producers, but energy enters as light and leaves as heat.

questions.prompt: Producers hold 5000 kJ and each step passes on 10% of the energy it receives. Which set shows the energy held at levels 1, 2, 3 and 4?
hints: A transfer of 10% means each level holds a tenth of the one below.
Check how each number compares with the one before it.
questions.onCorrect: Each level holds a tenth of the one below, so the energy falls by a factor of ten at every step.

misconceptions.feedback: That takes the same amount off at each step. A transfer of 10% passes on a tenth of what each level holds, so the amounts fall by a factor of ten.
That halves the energy at each step, which is a transfer of 50%. At 10% each level holds a tenth of the one below.

questions.prompt: The producers hold 2000 kJ. At an assumed 10% transfer at each step, how many kJ reach level 3?
hints: Level 3 is two steps above the producers.
Take 10% of the energy once, then take 10% of the result.
Multiply by 0.1 twice.
questions.onCorrect: The first step gives 2000 × 0.1 = 200 kJ and the second gives 200 × 0.1 = 20 kJ at level 3.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the energy at level 2, after one step. Level 3 is a further step on.
That is the energy held by the producers. Two steps with 10% transfer reduce it a good deal.
That subtracts 10% instead of taking 10%. At each step only a tenth of the energy passes on.

questions.prompt: Two lakes have producers that hold 9000 kJ. Lake X passes on 10% at each step and Lake Y passes on 20%. How do the energies at level 4 compare?
hints: Work out how much each lake passes on at the first step, then at the second and third.
Compare the factor by which Y's step differs from X's, and ask how many steps it applies to.

acceptedIdeas: About eight times as much in Y, since each of three steps doubles it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About eight times as much in Y, since each of three steps doubles it

choices.label: About twice as much in Y, since 20% is double the 10% rate of X
About eight times as much in Y, since each of three steps doubles it
The same in both, since the producers hold the same energy to begin with

questions.onCorrect: Y passes on twice the fraction at each of three steps, so it holds 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 times the energy at level 4.

misconceptions.feedback: The efficiency applies at every step. Three steps up, doubling it multiplies the result by 2 × 2 × 2 = 8.
The starting energy is the same, but the fraction passed on at each step differs, and the difference grows with every step.

questions.prompt: A consumer level is to receive 300 kJ. At an assumed 10% transfer, how many kJ must the level below hold?
hints: The level below supplies the energy, and only a tenth of it reaches the consumer level.
The consumer level holds one tenth of what the level below held.
Divide 300 by 0.10.
questions.onCorrect: The consumers receive a tenth of what the level below holds, so that level held 300 ÷ 0.10 = 3000 kJ.

misconceptions.feedback: That takes a tenth of the 300 kJ, which goes up a step and not down one. The level below held more than the consumers received.
That is the energy the consumer level is to receive. The level below must hold more than that.
Adding ten percent is not the reverse of taking ten percent. The level below held ten times what the consumers receive.

questions.prompt: A reserve has enough plants to feed 1,000 herbivores. Why can it support far fewer carnivores that eat those herbivores?
hints: Energy falls at every step up the chain.
Ask how much of the plants' energy a carnivore can receive.

acceptedIdeas: Only a small share of the energy at each level passes on to the next
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only a small share of the energy at each level passes on to the next

choices.label: Only a small share of the energy at each level passes on to the next
Carnivores need much more space than herbivores do
Carnivores use up more of the plants' energy in the first place

questions.onCorrect: Most of the energy at each level never reaches the next, so the levels above the herbivores hold too little to support many animals.

misconceptions.feedback: Space can matter, but the main limit is energy. Each level receives only a fraction of the energy held by the level below it.
Carnivores do not eat the plants. They receive only the fraction that the herbivores pass on.

questions.prompt: A student counts yeast in a small flask of nutrient broth each day. The counts, in thousands and invented for this question, are 2, 8, 30, 75, 110, 120 and 121. What is the best estimate of the flask's carrying capacity?
hints: Look at what the counts do near the end of the week.
The carrying capacity is a size that the population levels off near.

acceptedIdeas: About 120 thousand, where the counts level off
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 120 thousand, where the counts level off

choices.label: About 75 thousand, the count after the biggest rise
About 2 thousand, where the population began
About 120 thousand, where the counts level off

questions.onCorrect: The counts rise slowly, then quickly, then level off near 120 thousand, the largest population the flask can keep supporting.

misconceptions.feedback: The biggest one-day rise was from 30 to 75, but growth went on beyond it. The carrying capacity is the level the counts settle at.
That is the starting size. The carrying capacity is the largest population the flask can keep supporting.

questions.prompt: A closed population stays at 500 animals for ten years. A student says that no animals can have been born or have died in that time. What is wrong with that?
hints: The net change is births minus deaths.
Ask what net change results if the two are equal.

acceptedIdeas: Births can equal deaths, so the size holds steady as animals are replaced
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Births can equal deaths, so the size holds steady as animals are replaced

choices.label: Nothing is wrong, since any birth or any death would change the size
Births can equal deaths, so the size holds steady as animals are replaced
Deaths must have outnumbered births, since a steady size means a slow loss

questions.onCorrect: Equal births and deaths give a net change of zero, even though the individuals in the population are constantly replaced.

misconceptions.feedback: A birth adds one and a death takes one away, so equal numbers cancel and the size is unchanged.
If deaths outnumbered births the size would fall. A steady size means that the two are equal.

questions.prompt: A closed population starts at 70, with 16 births and 9 deaths. What is its final size?
hints: The new size is the starting size plus births minus deaths.
The starting size is 70.
Add the 16 births and take away the 9 deaths.
questions.onCorrect: The population begins at 70, gains 16 and loses 9, so it ends at 70 + 16 − 9 = 77.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the births but does not take away the deaths. Deaths reduce the population.
That takes the births away from the starting size instead of adding them. Births add to the population.
That is the net change, births minus deaths. The question asks for the final size, which includes the starting 70.

questions.prompt: A claim says fertiliser helps plants grow. Which measurement would let you test it?
hints: The claim is about growth, so choose something that changes as a plant grows.
It must be something you can measure with a ruler or a balance.

acceptedIdeas: Each plant's height in centimetres, at the start and the end
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each plant's height in centimetres, at the start and the end

choices.label: The mass of fertiliser given to each pot, in grams
Each plant's height in centimetres, at the start and the end
How healthy each plant looks, judged at the start and end

questions.onCorrect: Height can be measured the same way on every plant, and measuring it at the start as well as the end shows how much each one grew.

misconceptions.feedback: How healthy a plant looks is a judgement that two people can disagree about. A test needs a quantity that a ruler or a balance can give.
The amount of fertiliser is the thing being tested. The measurement has to be taken on the plants, to see whether they grew more.

questions.prompt: A gardener gives a fertiliser to the 10 pots nearest the window, which get more light, and none to the other 10. What should she use to decide which pots get the fertiliser, so that the two groups start out alike?
hints: The treated and control groups should be alike at the start.
Ask what would stop her own choice from favouring the pots with more light.

acceptedIdeas: random assignment
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Random assignment: a chance draw, so that the groups are alike on average.

questions.onCorrect: A random draw makes the groups alike on average, so a later difference can be put down to the fertiliser.

misconceptions.feedback: She already has a control group. The question asks how the pots are allocated to the two groups.
More pots is a separate matter. She needs a way of choosing that does not favour any pot.
Giving every pot the same light would help, but the question asks what should decide which pots get the treatment.

questions.prompt: Pots were assigned to fertiliser or control by a random draw. After three weeks the four treated pots grew 12, 13, 11 and 14 cm, and the four control pots grew 7, 8, 6 and 7 cm. Which conclusion do the results support?
hints: Compare the gap between the two groups with the spread inside each group.
Science does not claim to prove anything. Ask what these pots can and cannot show.

acceptedIdeas: The fertiliser probably helped here, as the two groups do not overlap
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The fertiliser probably helped here, as the two groups do not overlap

choices.label: The fertiliser has been proved to help every kind of plant to grow more
Nothing can be said, since each of the two groups has only four pots
The fertiliser probably helped here, as the two groups do not overlap

questions.onCorrect: Every treated pot grew more than any control pot, so chance alone is an unlikely explanation. The result supports the claim for these pots and does not prove it for all plants.

misconceptions.feedback: A result supports a claim and does not prove it. Eight pots of one kind of plant cannot show what would happen in every plant.
Four pots is a small sample, but the gap of about 5 cm between the groups is much larger than the spread within each group.

questions.prompt: Why report variability across independent pots as well as the mean?
hints: A mean hides how far the individual values spread.
Think about what the spread tells you about the replicates.

acceptedIdeas: It shows how consistent the results are
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Variability reveals whether the mean hides wide differences between replicates.

choices.label: It shows how consistent the results are
It makes a control unnecessary
It proves every plant behaves identically

questions.onCorrect: It shows how consistent the results are. A mean with a wide spread is a less reliable guide than one with a narrow spread.

misconceptions.feedback: Variability tells you about the spread among replicates. A control is still needed to show what would have happened without the treatment.
Variability exists because plants differ. Reporting it shows how much, and it does not prove that they behave identically.

questions.prompt: An old strand reads ATGC. Which is the new strand built against it, written in the same left-to-right order?
hints: Match each old base with its partner, in order.
The pairs are A with T and C with G.
Write the partners from left to right.

acceptedIdeas: TACG
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: TACG

choices.label: GCAT
TAGC
TACG

questions.onCorrect: TACG. Each old base is matched in turn: A with T, T with A, G with C and C with G.

misconceptions.feedback: Those are the right partners in reverse order. Write the new strand's bases from left to right, in the same order as the old strand.
A and T have been paired correctly, but G and C have been left as they were. G pairs with C and C pairs with G.

questions.prompt: A student says that copying doubles the number of chromosomes in a cell. What is the best reply?
hints: After copying, each chromosome consists of two joined halves.
Ask what is counted as one chromosome, and how many DNA molecules each one holds.

acceptedIdeas: It doubles the DNA molecules, but the joined copies still count as one chromosome
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It doubles the DNA molecules, but the joined copies still count as one chromosome

choices.label: That is right, because each chromosome becomes two separate chromosomes
It changes nothing until the cell divides, because the DNA is copied during division
It doubles the DNA molecules, but the joined copies still count as one chromosome

questions.onCorrect: Copying doubles the DNA molecules and leaves the number of chromosomes unchanged, since the sister chromatids count together.

misconceptions.feedback: The two copies stay attached as sister chromatids, and the pair is still counted as one chromosome until they separate.

questions.prompt: A membrane is permeable to water but not to a dye. 9 dye units are on the left and 3 on the right. What happens to the dye on the left over a long time?
hints: Ask which substance the question is about, the water or the dye.
A substance that cannot cross cannot be shared out between the sides.

acceptedIdeas: It stays at 9 units, because the dye cannot cross
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It stays at 9 units, because the dye cannot cross

choices.label: It stays at 9 units, because the dye cannot cross
It falls to 6 units, because the dye spreads out evenly
It rises above 9 units, because the water draws more dye in

questions.onCorrect: The dye cannot cross, so its amount on each side never changes, however freely the water moves.

misconceptions.feedback: The dye would settle at 6 on each side only if it could cross. This membrane lets water through and holds the dye back.
