questions.prompt: Put these steps of a fair test of a fertiliser in order.
hints: You cannot measure growth without a starting value.
The groups have to be formed, by chance, before the treatment begins.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The claim is made measurable first, starting heights are recorded, plants are assigned by a random draw, both groups are treated alike apart from the fertiliser, and the average growth of the groups is compared last.

items: State the quantity to measure, such as height in centimetres
Assign the plants to fertiliser or control by a random draw
Treat both groups alike apart from the fertiliser
Compare the average growth of the two groups

questions.onCorrect: The measure and the baseline come first, chance forms the groups, the treatment follows, and the comparison comes last because it needs every measurement.

questions.prompt: Frog counts are higher at ponds with more reeds. Which study would best test whether reeds cause there to be more frogs?
hints: An observed pattern is an association, so ask what else could produce it besides the reeds.
To separate the reeds from everything else you have to change the reeds and keep the rest alike.

acceptedIdeas: Change the reed cover at randomly chosen ponds and compare with unchanged ponds
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Change the reed cover at randomly chosen ponds and compare with unchanged ponds

choices.label: Count the frogs at many more ponds, to see whether the pattern holds
Compare the ponds that already have the most reeds with those that have the fewest
Change the reed cover at randomly chosen ponds and compare with unchanged ponds

questions.onCorrect: Only an experiment that changes the reed cover while the ponds are otherwise alike can separate the reeds from shade, pond size and other differences.

misconceptions.feedback: More ponds make the pattern clearer but cannot remove other explanations. Shade or pond size could still explain both.
That repeats the observation. Those ponds may also differ in shade, depth or other things.

questions.prompt: Plant A, given fertiliser, grows from 4 cm to 19 cm. Plant B, given none, grows from 12 cm to 22 cm. A student says B did better because it ended taller. What is wrong with that?
hints: Plants do not all begin at the same height.
Work out how far each plant grew, as the later height minus the starting height.

acceptedIdeas: Growth is the change from the starting height, and A grew 15 cm to B's 10 cm
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Growth is the change from the starting height, and A grew 15 cm to B's 10 cm

choices.label: Nothing is wrong, because the taller plant is the one that grew more
Growth is the change from the starting height, and A grew 15 cm to B's 10 cm
Plants should be compared at the start and not at the end, since final heights vary

questions.onCorrect: Plant A grew 19 − 4 = 15 cm and plant B grew 22 − 12 = 10 cm, so A grew more even though B ended taller.

misconceptions.feedback: Plant B began 8 cm taller, so its final height hides how little it grew. Growth is the change from where each plant started.
Both heights matter. Growth is the later value minus the starting value, and that is the fair measure.

questions.prompt: An ecologist measures a lake chain. The producers hold 12000 kJ, the herbivores hold 1800 kJ and the carnivores hold 270 kJ. Which statement fits these measurements?
hints: Work out the herbivores' energy as a fraction of the producers' energy.
Then do the same for the carnivores and the herbivores.

acceptedIdeas: About 15% passes on at each step, a little above the 10% rule of thumb
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 15% passes on at each step, a little above the 10% rule of thumb

choices.label: About 10% passes on at each step, exactly as the rule of thumb says it must
About 15% passes on at each step, a little above the 10% rule of thumb
About 85% passes on at each step, since only 15% of the energy is lost

questions.onCorrect: 1800 ÷ 12000 and 270 ÷ 1800 both give 0.15, so about 15% passes on, which shows that 10% is a rule of thumb and not a law.

misconceptions.feedback: The rule of thumb is not a law. Here 1800 ÷ 12000 is 0.15, and 270 ÷ 1800 is also 0.15.
That reverses it. The herbivores hold 15% of the producers' energy, so 15% passes on and 85% does not.

questions.prompt: A herbivore eats plants, and a predator then eats the herbivore. Which of these reaches the predator, and which does not?
hints: The predator can use only energy that became part of the herbivore's body.
Ask of each item whether it ended up in the herbivore's tissue.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The energy given off as heat, the parts never eaten and the food passed out undigested do not reach the predator. The muscle and the fat do.

items.label: Energy used in the herbivore's respiration and given off as heat
items.explanation: It leaves the chain as heat and cannot be passed on.

items.label: Parts of the plants that the herbivore never eats, such as roots
items.explanation: Food that is not eaten never becomes part of the herbivore.

items.label: Food that passes through the herbivore undigested
items.explanation: It did not become part of the herbivore, so there is nothing for the predator to eat.

items.label: Muscle that the herbivore built from its food
items.explanation: It is body tissue, and the predator eats it.

items.label: Fat stored in the herbivore's body
items.explanation: It is part of the body that the predator eats.

questions.onCorrect: Only energy built into the herbivore's body can reach the predator. What is respired, left uneaten or passed out undigested does not.

questions.prompt: A cow eats 120 kilograms of grain and gains 15 kilograms of body mass. Which explanation of the difference fits best?
hints: Think about what the cow's cells do with the energy of their food.
Some of what an animal eats is never digested.

acceptedIdeas: Much is used in respiration and lost as heat, or passes out undigested
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Much is used in respiration and lost as heat, or passes out undigested

choices.label: Much is used in respiration and lost as heat, or passes out undigested
The grain holds little energy until the cow has digested it fully
Energy is destroyed as food is digested, so most of it is gone for good

questions.onCorrect: Most of the energy is used in respiration and leaves as heat, and some of the food is not digested, so only a small share becomes body mass.

misconceptions.feedback: The grain holds the energy the cow takes in. The shortfall comes from what happens to that energy: use, heat and waste.
Energy is not destroyed. It is used in respiration and given off as heat, and some food passes through the animal undigested.

questions.prompt: A student tests whether temperature changes how fast an enzyme works. Which of these should she change on purpose, which keep the same in every sample, and which measure?
hints: Ask of each item whether it is the thing being tested, the result, or something that could spoil the comparison.
A fair test lets only one thing differ.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: She changes the temperature, keeps the enzyme amount, substrate volume, time and enzyme the same, and measures the product made.

items.label: The temperature of each sample
items.explanation: It is the one thing the test is about, so it is the only thing that should differ.

items.label: The amount of enzyme in each sample
items.explanation: If it differed, a difference in rate could come from the enzyme and not from the temperature.

items.label: The volume of substrate solution in each sample
items.explanation: A different volume could change the rate and confuse the result.

items.label: How much product forms in the time allowed
items.explanation: It is the result, and it shows how fast the enzyme worked.

items.label: How long each sample is left to react
items.explanation: Unequal times would give unequal amounts of product whatever the temperature.

items.label: Which enzyme is used
items.explanation: Another enzyme could have a different optimum, so every sample uses the same one.

questions.onCorrect: Only the temperature differs between samples. Everything else that could change the rate is held the same, and the product made is the result.

questions.prompt: Enzyme A is an enzyme from a human cell, and it speeds up as it is warmed from 10°C to 40°C. What happens to its rate at 55°C?
hints: Think about what high temperatures do to a folded protein.
A rate falls when the enzyme can no longer bind its substrate.

acceptedIdeas: It falls
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It falls

choices.label: It rises further
It stays at the rate it had at 40°C
It falls

questions.onCorrect: By 55°C an enzyme like A has begun to lose its shape, and the substrate fits less well.

misconceptions.feedback: Warmth speeds an enzyme up only until its shape starts to change. Beyond that, the active site no longer fits the substrate.
The rate is not fixed. Once the temperature is high enough to change the enzyme's shape, the rate changes with it.

questions.prompt: The enzyme in saliva that breaks down starch is mixed with a protein, and nothing happens to the protein. What best explains this?
hints: Each enzyme works on only one substrate or a few closely related ones.
Ask what decides whether a substrate can bind.

acceptedIdeas: The protein does not fit the enzyme's active site
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The protein does not fit the enzyme's active site

choices.label: The enzyme has been used up by an earlier reaction
The protein does not fit the enzyme's active site
The enzyme only works once it has been warmed above body temperature

questions.onCorrect: Binding depends on the shape and chemistry of the active site, so an enzyme that breaks down starch cannot act on a protein.

misconceptions.feedback: An enzyme comes out of a reaction unchanged. What limits it is whether the substrate fits its active site.
Warmth speeds an enzyme up only until its shape begins to change, and temperature does not decide which substrate it can act on.

questions.prompt: Not all the energy from fuel ends up in ATP. In what form does much of the rest disperse?
hints: Think about why your body stays warm.
It is the form of energy that spreads out as warmth.

acceptedIdeas: heat
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Energy that is not transferred to ATP disperses as heat.

questions.onCorrect: As heat. Respiration transfers part of the fuel's energy to ATP and disperses the rest as warmth.

misconceptions.feedback: That is not what a cell disperses its spare energy as. The form is the one that keeps a mammal's body warm.
ATP is where part of the energy goes. The question asks about the rest, which is not captured in it.

questions.prompt: A student compares oxygen use by peas at two temperatures. In three minutes the jar at 10°C loses 4 units and the jar at 25°C loses 10, and a blank jar at each temperature loses 1. Which conclusion do the readings support?
hints: Take each blank off its own jar before you compare the temperatures.
Both blanks lost the same amount, so they cannot account for a difference between the jars.

acceptedIdeas: The peas respired faster at 25°C, and the blanks do not explain the gap
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The peas respired faster at 25°C, and the blanks do not explain the gap

choices.label: The peas respired faster at 25°C, and the blanks do not explain the gap
The peas respire only when warm, because the cold jar lost less oxygen
The result is unreliable, because the blanks lost some oxygen

questions.onCorrect: Once the blanks are taken off, the peas used about 3 units at 10°C and 9 at 25°C, so they respired about three times as fast when warm.

misconceptions.feedback: The cold jar lost 3 units more than its blank, so the peas respired there too. They did so more slowly.
A blank that loses a little oxygen is expected. It lost the same at both temperatures, so taking it off each jar leaves a clear difference.

questions.prompt: You breathe out carbon dioxide. Which molecule in your cells did its carbon atoms come from?
hints: Look at the equation: which input contains carbon?
Oxygen is what a cell takes in. Ask what it is used for.

acceptedIdeas: glucose
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: From the glucose your cells broke down for fuel.

questions.onCorrect: The carbon atoms of the glucose leave in carbon dioxide, which the blood carries to the lungs to be breathed out.

misconceptions.feedback: Oxygen has no carbon atoms. The carbon comes from the fuel that the oxygen is used to break down.
Water is made in respiration, but it contains no carbon. The carbon in the breath comes from the fuel.
Air carries the gas out, but the carbon dioxide is made in your cells. Its carbon atoms come from the fuel they broke down.

questions.prompt: In three minutes a jar of peas loses 9 units of oxygen. A blank jar set up the same way, with no peas, loses 8. What should the student conclude?
hints: The organisms' own use is the change in their jar minus the change in the blank.
Compare how much the blank lost with how much the peas' jar lost.

acceptedIdeas: The peas used little oxygen, and most of the fall has another cause
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The peas used little oxygen, and most of the fall has another cause

choices.label: The peas used 9 units, because the blank is only a rough guide
The blank is faulty and should be ignored, since peas must use oxygen
The peas used little oxygen, and most of the fall has another cause

questions.onCorrect: The blank lost 8 of the 9 units, so the peas used only about 1. Most of the fall came from the set-up, such as a leak.

misconceptions.feedback: The blank shows what changes without peas, and here it accounts for 8 of the 9 units.
A blank that loses oxygen is doing its job. It shows that the set-up itself lost almost as much as the peas' jar did.

questions.prompt: A cell has a plasma membrane and DNA, but no nucleus and no mitochondria. Which kind of cell is it?
hints: Check which parts the cell has and which it lacks.
Only one of these kinds of cell keeps its DNA in a nucleoid.

acceptedIdeas: A bacterium
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A bacterium

choices.label: An animal cell
A plant cell
A bacterium

questions.onCorrect: A bacterium. No nucleus and no mitochondria is the bacterial design.

misconceptions.feedback: An animal cell has a nucleus and mitochondria, and this cell has neither.
A plant cell has a nucleus and mitochondria, as an animal cell does, and this cell has neither.

questions.prompt: A plant is given CO₂ whose carbon atoms are labelled. Which molecule do the labelled carbon atoms end up in?
hints: The labelled carbon goes where the carbon goes.
The carbon from CO₂ is joined into the product of photosynthesis.

acceptedIdeas: Glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, the sugar the plant builds
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, the sugar the plant builds

choices.label: Oxygen, O₂, because the plant gives off oxygen
Glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, the sugar the plant builds
Water, H₂O, because the plant also takes water in

questions.onCorrect: Glucose, the sugar. The labelled carbon atoms are built into it.

misconceptions.feedback: Oxygen gas contains no carbon. The labelled carbon atoms end up in the product that is built from them.
Water contains no carbon, so labelled carbon cannot end up there.

questions.prompt: A student wants to test whether carbon dioxide limits how fast pondweed photosynthesises. She gives one tank extra carbon dioxide and counts the oxygen bubbles from each. Which things should she keep the same in both tanks?
hints: Only the thing being tested should differ between the tanks.
Light and temperature also change the rate of photosynthesis.

acceptedIdeas: The light, the temperature and the pondweed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The light, the temperature and the pondweed

choices.label: The amount of carbon dioxide dissolved in the water
The light, the temperature and the pondweed
The number of bubbles counted over the same time

questions.onCorrect: Only the carbon dioxide differs. Light and temperature also limit the rate, so keeping them the same lets any change be credited to the carbon dioxide.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the one thing she changes on purpose. If it were the same in both tanks there would be no test.
The bubbles are the result she measures. Forcing them to match would leave nothing to show.

questions.prompt: Which of these happen in meiosis I, and which in meiosis II?
hints: Meiosis I separates the two members of each pair, and meiosis II separates the two copies of each chromosome.
Ask of each statement whether the chromatids are still joined at that point.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Meiosis I separates the homologous chromosomes, halves the number and leaves chromatids joined. Meiosis II separates the sister chromatids and gives four cells, much as mitosis would.

items.label: The two members of each homologous pair go to different cells
items.explanation: Meiosis I separates whole chromosomes, one from each pair into each cell.

items.label: The sister chromatids of each chromosome are pulled apart
items.explanation: Meiosis II separates chromatids, much as mitosis does.

items.label: The number of chromosomes in each cell is halved
items.explanation: The halving happens when the members of each pair are separated.

items.label: Each cell that forms holds chromosomes made of two chromatids
items.explanation: The chromatids are still joined at the end of the first division.

items.label: Each of the four cells that form holds single-chromatid chromosomes
items.explanation: The chromatids have separated, which leaves four haploid cells.

items.label: It works much like mitosis
items.explanation: The chromatids of each chromosome are shared out, as they are in mitosis.

questions.onCorrect: The first division separates homologous chromosomes and halves the number. The second separates sister chromatids and gives four cells.

questions.prompt: Two brothers who are not twins have the same parents but different combinations of chromosomes. Which part of meiosis helps to explain this?
hints: In meiosis I, which member of a pair goes to which end is decided by chance.
Fertilisation then joins one of many possible sperm with one of many possible eggs.

acceptedIdeas: Each pair lines up independently, so each gamete gets a different mix
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each pair lines up independently, so each gamete gets a different mix

choices.label: Each pair lines up independently, so each gamete gets a different mix
Meiosis copies the DNA a different number of times in each gamete
Meiosis II gives each child a different number of chromosomes

questions.onCorrect: Chance in how each pair lines up, and the swapping of segments in crossing over, makes every gamete different. Fertilisation adds more variety.

misconceptions.feedback: The DNA is copied once before the two divisions, in every meiosis. The variety comes from how the chromosomes are shared out.
Every child receives the same number, 46 in humans. What differs is which member of each pair goes into a gamete.

questions.prompt: In a species with 12 chromosomes in each body cell, a student says that gametes carry 12 too, and that fertilisation keeps the number equal. What is wrong with that?
hints: A gamete is haploid, with one set.
Fertilisation brings two haploid sets together.

acceptedIdeas: Gametes carry 6, and fertilisation joins two sets of 6 to make 12
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Gametes carry 6, and fertilisation joins two sets of 6 to make 12

choices.label: Nothing is wrong, since fertilisation halves the number
Gametes carry 24, so that fertilisation halves them to 12
Gametes carry 6, and fertilisation joins two sets of 6 to make 12

questions.onCorrect: Meiosis halves the number to 6 in each gamete, and fertilisation joins two of them to restore 12.

misconceptions.feedback: Fertilisation joins two gametes and so adds their chromosomes together. Meiosis is what halves the number.
Gametes are haploid, with half the diploid number. They carry 6, and fertilisation doubles that to 12.

questions.prompt: In one species the egg and sperm cells each carry 5 chromosomes. How many chromosomes would you expect in one of its skin cells?
hints: A gamete carries one set, and fertilisation brings two together.
Skin cells descend from the fertilised egg by mitosis, which keeps the chromosome number.

acceptedIdeas: Ten, because the first cell combined two sets of five
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ten, because the first cell combined two sets of five

choices.label: Five, because every cell of an animal has the same number
Ten, because the first cell combined two sets of five
Twenty, because the DNA is copied before fertilisation

questions.onCorrect: Fertilisation joins two haploid sets, so every body cell is diploid, with twice the number of chromosomes of a gamete.

misconceptions.feedback: Skin cells are diploid. The fertilised egg combined the egg's five with the sperm's five, and its descendants keep that number.
Copying doubles the DNA molecules and leaves the chromosome count alone. A body cell has two sets, 5 + 5 = 10.

questions.prompt: Cell P has 8 chromosomes holding 8 DNA molecules. Cell Q, from the same tissue, has 8 chromosomes holding 16 DNA molecules. Which statement is right?
hints: Divide each cell's DNA molecules by its chromosomes to see how many each chromosome holds.
Copying changes the number of DNA molecules but not the number of chromosomes.

acceptedIdeas: Cell Q has copied its DNA, so each chromosome has two sister chromatids
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Cell Q has copied its DNA, so each chromosome has two sister chromatids

choices.label: Cell Q has twice as many chromosomes as cell P, because its DNA is copied
Cell P is about to divide, because it holds fewer DNA molecules
Cell Q has copied its DNA, so each chromosome has two sister chromatids

questions.onCorrect: Q holds two DNA molecules in each chromosome, the two sister chromatids, so it has copied its DNA and P has not.

misconceptions.feedback: Both cells have 8 chromosomes. Copying doubles the DNA molecules and leaves the chromosome number unchanged.
A cell divides after its DNA is copied, so Q is the one nearer to dividing. P has not copied its DNA yet.

questions.prompt: One cell completes four ideal rounds of division, with every descendant dividing each round. How many cells result?
hints: Each round doubles the number of cells.
Start with one cell and double it once for each round.
Double four times in a row.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The sequence is 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 16.

questions.onCorrect: Each round doubles the count: 1, 2, 4, 8, then 16 cells after four rounds.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number after three rounds. A fourth round doubles it again.
That adds 3 each round. Every cell divides, so the count doubles each round.
That is the number of rounds. The question asks for the number of cells.

questions.prompt: A scientist counts the dividing cells in two tissues from a healthy adult, the lining of the gut and the brain. Many gut cells are dividing and almost no brain cells are. What does this suggest?
hints: In an adult, division replaces cells that wear out.
Ask which of the two tissues loses cells all the time.

acceptedIdeas: Gut cells are replaced by division, while most nerve cells hardly divide
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Gut cells are replaced by division, while most nerve cells hardly divide

choices.label: Gut cells are replaced by division, while most nerve cells hardly divide
The gut lining must be cancerous, because so many of its cells are dividing
The brain cells must have lost their DNA, because they hardly ever divide

questions.onCorrect: Division is controlled: tissues that lose cells replace them, and cells such as most nerve cells in the brain hardly divide at all.

misconceptions.feedback: Division that replaces worn-out cells is controlled. Cancer is what follows when the control fails and a cell divides without limit.
A cell that does not divide still holds all its DNA. Most nerve cells hardly divide at all.

questions.prompt: A scientist grows 10 separate cultures of bacteria and adds a virus that kills them to each. The numbers of survivors, invented for this question, are 0, 0, 3, 0, 212, 0, 1, 0, 0 and 45. Which idea fits this pattern?
hints: If the virus caused resistance, what would you expect each culture to show?
A resistant mutant that arose early leaves many descendants, and one that arose late leaves few.

acceptedIdeas: Resistance arose by chance, at random times before the virus was added
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Resistance arose by chance, at random times before the virus was added

choices.label: The virus made each culture resistant, so every culture should have had a similar number
The counts are too uneven to say anything, so the experiment shows nothing
Resistance arose by chance, at random times before the virus was added

questions.onCorrect: Uneven counts fit mutations that arose at random times before the virus was added. Luria and Delbrück used this pattern in 1943.

misconceptions.feedback: If the virus caused resistance, the counts would be alike. Counts this uneven fit resistant bacteria arising at random times before the virus.
The uneven counts are the evidence. A mutation at a random time leaves a few cultures with many survivors and most with none.

questions.prompt: A mutation arises in a cell that makes eggs and is inherited by a child. Put these steps in order.
hints: The mutation has to be in a gamete before it can be in a child.
Fertilisation turns the gamete into the first cell of the child.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The mutation arises in an egg-making cell, the egg carrying it takes part in fertilisation, the first cell of the child then holds it, and every cell that descends from that cell carries it.

items: A mutation arises in a cell that makes gametes
The gamete that carries it takes part in fertilisation
The mutation is present in the first cell of the child
Every cell that descends from that first cell carries the mutation

questions.onCorrect: A mutation in a gamete is carried into the first cell of the child and copied into every cell that descends from it.

questions.prompt: Do mutations arise because an organism needs them?
hints: Think about whether a mutation can know what a cell needs.
Mutations are changes in DNA that happen by chance.

acceptedIdeas: No, they arise by chance, whether they turn out useful or not
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, they arise by chance, whether they turn out useful or not

choices.label: Yes, a mutation appears once the environment makes it useful
No, they arise by chance, whether they turn out useful or not
Only in bacteria, which change their DNA when a virus attacks them

questions.onCorrect: Whether a mutation helps is decided afterwards, by the environment its carriers live in.

misconceptions.feedback: A mutation is a chance change in DNA and cannot know what a cell needs. Whether it helps is decided only afterwards.
Luria and Delbrück found that resistant bacteria arose at random times before the virus was added, so bacteria do not make the mutations they need either.

questions.prompt: A man builds large muscles by lifting weights for years. Why does this not make large muscles more common among his descendants through selection?
hints: Selection can change a population only through differences that offspring inherit.
Ask whether his children receive his muscle or only his DNA.

acceptedIdeas: The muscle came from his own life and is not passed on through DNA
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The muscle came from his own life and is not passed on through DNA

choices.label: Selection acts only on traits that harm the organism that carries them
Large muscles cannot help anyone to leave more surviving offspring
The muscle came from his own life and is not passed on through DNA

questions.onCorrect: Only heritable differences can be selected. A trait acquired in one lifetime is not passed on through DNA.

misconceptions.feedback: Selection acts on any heritable difference in survival or reproduction, whether it helps or hinders. The problem here is that the muscle was not inherited.
Whether a trait helps is a separate matter. Selection needs a difference that is inherited, and built-up muscle is not passed on through DNA.

questions.prompt: A pond's carrying capacity depends on its food, water, shelter and space. Which of these would raise it, and which would lower it?
hints: Carrying capacity is set by the resources the habitat provides.
Ask whether each change gives the population more or less food, water, shelter or space.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The drought, the competing species and the lost shore lower it. The new food supply, the new shallow water and the spreading reeds raise it.

items.label: A drought dries up half of the pond
items.explanation: Less water and space can support fewer animals.

items.label: A new food supply washes in from a stream
items.explanation: More food can support a larger population.

items.label: A competing species that eats the same food arrives
items.explanation: The newcomer takes a share of the food.

items.label: Part of the shore is lost to building
items.explanation: Less habitat is left for the population.

items.label: A new area of shallow water opens up along the shore
items.explanation: More space and shelter can support more animals.

items.label: Reeds that give shelter spread along the shore
items.explanation: More shelter can support a larger population.

questions.onCorrect: A change that adds resources raises the carrying capacity, and one that removes resources or adds a competitor lowers it.

questions.prompt: A student plots a population against time and gets an S-shape that levels off at the top. She says the population has stopped reproducing there. What is wrong with that?
hints: The net change is births minus deaths.
Near the carrying capacity births tend to fall and deaths tend to rise.

acceptedIdeas: At the top births and deaths are roughly equal, so the size stops changing
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: At the top births and deaths are roughly equal, so the size stops changing

choices.label: At the top births and deaths are roughly equal, so the size stops changing
Nothing is wrong, because a flat curve means that no births are happening
The curve should keep rising, because reproduction speeds up as numbers grow

questions.onCorrect: Near the carrying capacity births fall and deaths rise until they balance, so the population levels off without anything having stopped.

misconceptions.feedback: A flat curve means the size is steady. That happens when births and deaths balance, and individuals can still be born.
Growth slows as food and space run short, so the population levels off near its carrying capacity.

questions.prompt: A pond is 20 square metres. A patch of lilies covers 1 square metre today and doubles its area every day, with nothing to stop it. On which day from today does the patch first cover more than 20 square metres?
hints: Write the area for each day: day 0 is 1 square metre.
The area doubles every day, so the next area is twice the one before.
Keep doubling until the area is more than 20.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The area is 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 on days 0 to 4, and 32 on day 5, which is over 20.

questions.onCorrect: The area is 16 on day 4, which is under 20, and 32 on day 5, so day 5 is the first day over 20.

misconceptions.feedback: On day 4 the patch covers 16 square metres, which is not yet more than 20. The next doubling takes it over.
That is the area of the pond, not a number of days. Keep doubling the area day by day and count the days.
Doubling each day is much faster than adding a fixed area each day. Write out the area for each day and watch it double.

questions.prompt: As the pond becomes crowded, what happens to the patch's growth each day?
hints: Think about what happens to the space and nutrients as the patch spreads.
The pond is not unlimited, and a patch that covers more of it has less left to spread into.

acceptedIdeas: It slows down
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It slows down

choices.label: It slows down
It keeps speeding up, as the doubling does
It stays the same each day

questions.onCorrect: As the pond fills there is less space and fewer nutrients, so the patch grows by less each day.

misconceptions.feedback: The growth is not constant once the patch starts to fill the pond, because the space left for it keeps shrinking.
The patch is spreading into a pond whose size does not change, and each day it has less free space left to spread into.

questions.prompt: For Aa × Aa, what percentage of offspring is expected to show the dominant phenotype?
hints: Draw the four boxes for the cross.
The dominant phenotype shows in any box that has at least one A.
Count those boxes and divide by four.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: AA, Aa and Aa show the dominant trait: 3 ÷ 4 = 75%.

questions.onCorrect: Three of the four boxes, AA, Aa and Aa, contain A and show the dominant trait, which is 3 ÷ 4 = 75%.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the share that are aa, with the recessive trait. The dominant trait shows in the other boxes as well.
That counts only the Aa boxes. AA offspring show the dominant trait too.
The aa box shows the recessive trait, so not every offspring shows the dominant one.

questions.prompt: Two parents both show the dominant trait, but their child shows the recessive trait. What word describes each parent's genotype?
hints: The child's genotype must be aa to show the recessive trait.
The child received one a from each parent.
Each parent shows the dominant trait, so each must also carry a dominant allele.

acceptedIdeas: heterozygous
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each parent must carry one recessive allele without showing it, so each is heterozygous.

questions.onCorrect: Heterozygous. Each parent passed on a, and each shows the dominant trait, so each must be Aa.

misconceptions.feedback: A parent with two dominant alleles could pass on only A. To have an aa child, each parent must carry a as well.
An aa parent would show the recessive trait itself, and both parents here show the dominant one.

questions.prompt: In a food web an arrow points from a rabbit to a fox. Which statement about the two animals is true?
hints: Think about which of the two is the food.
An arrow starts at the food and ends at the one that eats it.

acceptedIdeas: The fox eats the rabbit, because the arrow points to the eater
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The fox eats the rabbit, because the arrow points to the eater

choices.label: The fox eats the rabbit, because the arrow points to the eater
The rabbit eats the fox, because the arrow starts at the eater
Neither eats the other, because an arrow only shows they share a habitat

questions.onCorrect: The fox eats the rabbit. An arrow points from the food to the organism that eats it.

misconceptions.feedback: The arrow starts at the rabbit, so the rabbit is the food. The organism the arrow points to is the one that eats it.
An arrow in a food web is a feeding link, so it shows which organism eats which.

questions.prompt: Suppose every decomposer in a meadow disappeared. What would you expect to happen?
hints: Think about where the nutrients in dead remains go.
Producers take up nutrients from the soil and water.

acceptedIdeas: Dead material would pile up and producers would lack nutrients
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Dead material would pile up and producers would lack nutrients

choices.label: Energy would pile up, and the producers would grow faster as a result
Dead material would pile up and producers would lack nutrients
Very little, since producers make all their own food from light

questions.onCorrect: Decomposers return the nutrients of dead material to the soil and water, so without them producers would eventually run short.

misconceptions.feedback: Decomposers do not supply energy to producers. They return nutrients, and without them the nutrients stay locked in dead remains.
Producers make sugar from light, but they still take nutrients from the soil and water, and decomposers are what return them.

questions.prompt: A disease kills most of the zooplankton in a pond, and the zooplankton eat the algae. What happens to the amount of algae at first?
hints: Follow the arrow from the algae to the zooplankton.
The zooplankton are the ones that eat the algae.
Ask what losing most of the zooplankton does to the amount of algae that is eaten.

acceptedIdeas: It rises
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It rises

choices.label: It rises
It falls
It stays the same

questions.onCorrect: Far fewer algae are being eaten, so their amount rises at first.

misconceptions.feedback: The arrow runs from the algae to the zooplankton, so the zooplankton eat the algae, and losing most of them means far less algae is eaten.
The zooplankton were eating the algae, so losing most of them changes how much algae is eaten, and the algae change with it.

questions.prompt: A compartment of volume 4 holds 20 units of trapped solute. Water leaves until its volume is 2. What is its concentration now?
hints: The solute stays at 20 while the volume changes.
The volume is now 2.
Divide the amount of solute by the new volume.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The solute stays at 20: 20 ÷ 2 = 10 units per volume.

questions.onCorrect: Water leaving shrinks the volume to 2 while the 20 units stay put, so the concentration rises from 5 to 10.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the concentration before the water left, 20 units in a volume of 4. Losing water raises it.
That is the amount of solute, which has not changed. Concentration is the amount divided by the volume.
Multiplying gives a number with no meaning here. Concentration is the amount divided by the volume.

questions.prompt: A jug holds 6 spoonfuls of syrup in 2 litres of drink. You top it up with water, adding no more syrup, until it holds 4 litres. How many spoonfuls of syrup are there per litre now?
hints: The syrup does not leave the jug, so its amount does not change.
Only the volume has changed, from 2 litres to 4 litres.
Divide the 6 spoonfuls by the new volume.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The syrup is still 6 spoonfuls. 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5 spoonfuls per litre.

questions.onCorrect: The syrup is still 6 spoonfuls, now shared through 4 litres, so the drink holds 1.5 spoonfuls per litre.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the concentration before the top-up, 6 spoonfuls in 2 litres. Adding water changes the volume, so the concentration changes.
That is the number of spoonfuls, which has not changed. The question asks how many there are per litre.
That is the number of litres that were added. The question asks for spoonfuls of syrup per litre of drink.

questions.prompt: Four equal potato strips sit for an hour in sugar solutions of rising strength, A to D, and the sugar cannot cross the cell membranes. Strip A, in plain water, gained 6% of its mass and B gained 2%. Strip C lost 3% and D lost 9%. What do the results show?
hints: A strip that gains mass has gained water, and a strip that loses mass has lost water.
Between which two solutions does the change flip from a gain to a loss?

acceptedIdeas: The potato cells hold about as much solute as a solution between B and C
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The potato cells hold about as much solute as a solution between B and C

choices.label: Sugar left the potato in C and D, which is why those strips lost mass
Water entered the cells in every solution, since cells always take water in
The potato cells hold about as much solute as a solution between B and C

questions.onCorrect: Water entered the cells in A and B and left them in C and D. Somewhere between B and C the solution matches the cells, so no net water moves.

misconceptions.feedback: The sugar could not cross the membranes. The mass changed because water crossed, and in C and D it left the cells.
Strips C and D lost mass, so water left their cells. Water moves towards the side with more solute, which in C and D is outside.

questions.prompt: Two sets of three pots both have a mean growth of 9 cm. Set X grew 8, 9 and 10 cm and set Y grew 2, 9 and 16 cm. What does the difference between the sets show?
hints: Compare how far the pots in each set lie from the mean.
A mean hides how far the individual values are spread.

acceptedIdeas: X is more consistent, so its mean is the better guide
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: X is more consistent, so its mean is the better guide

choices.label: Y is the better set, because its pots cover a wider range
X is more consistent, so its mean is the better guide
There is no difference, because the means are the same

questions.onCorrect: Both means are 9 cm, but X's pots stay close to it and Y's do not. Reporting the spread as well as the mean shows how consistent the results are.

misconceptions.feedback: A wide spread means the pots behave very differently, so the mean says little about any one of them.
Two sets can share a mean and still differ a great deal. The spread shows how consistent the results are.

questions.prompt: A chemical stops every ribosome in a cell from working. In which cells would protein-making stop?
hints: A bacterium has no mitochondria and no nucleus, yet it still makes proteins.
Ask which cells have ribosomes, and then which of them would be affected.

acceptedIdeas: In every kind of cell, bacteria as well as animal and plant cells
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: In every kind of cell, bacteria as well as animal and plant cells

choices.label: In every kind of cell, bacteria as well as animal and plant cells
Only in cells with a nucleus, since the nucleus holds the instructions
Only in cells with mitochondria, since they supply the energy

questions.onCorrect: Every cell must make proteins, so every cell has ribosomes and every cell would be affected.

misconceptions.feedback: A bacterium has no nucleus and still makes proteins on ribosomes. Every cell has them.
Mitochondria are a eukaryotic feature, but bacteria have ribosomes too. Protein-making would stop in all of them.

questions.prompt: Leaf B makes twice as much glucose as leaf A in the same hour. How does the carbon dioxide it takes in compare?
hints: Each glucose holds six carbon atoms, and each carbon dioxide molecule holds one.
Atoms are rearranged and never made or lost.

acceptedIdeas: It takes in twice as much, since each glucose needs six
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It takes in twice as much, since each glucose needs six

choices.label: It takes in the same, since the carbon is used again and again
It takes in less than twice as much, since light does some of the work
It takes in twice as much, since each glucose needs six

questions.onCorrect: Each glucose holds six carbon atoms that all came from carbon dioxide, so twice the glucose needs twice the carbon dioxide.

misconceptions.feedback: Carbon atoms are not made or lost, so every glucose needs its own six from the air. Leaf B builds twice as many.
Light supplies energy and adds no atoms. All the carbon in the extra glucose has to come from carbon dioxide.

questions.prompt: Enzyme D's rates at 20, 30, 45 and 60°C are 4, 10, 7 and 2 units per minute. At which of these temperatures is the enzyme closest to its optimum?
hints: The optimum is the temperature at which the rate is highest.
Find the largest of the four rates first.
Then find the temperature at which it was measured.
questions.onCorrect: The rate climbs to 10 units per minute at 30°C and has fallen to 2 by 60°C, because the enzyme is being denatured.

misconceptions.feedback: At 20°C the rate is only 4, and a warmer temperature gave a higher rate.
At 45°C the rate is 7, and a cooler temperature gave a higher rate than that.
At 60°C the rate has fallen to 2, because the enzyme is being denatured, so the optimum lies below it.

questions.prompt: A leaf in a warm room photosynthesises at a rate of 8 at light level 60 and still at 8 at light level 80. What is limiting its rate at light level 80?
hints: Ask what happened to the rate when the light was raised.
A flat part of the curve means that a factor other than light has become the limit.

acceptedIdeas: Carbon dioxide, which is in short supply
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Carbon dioxide, which is in short supply

choices.label: Nothing, because the leaf is at the highest rate any leaf can reach
Light, because the leaf needs more of it
Carbon dioxide, which is in short supply

questions.onCorrect: Extra light left the rate unchanged, so light is no longer the limiting factor, and the short supply of carbon dioxide is.

misconceptions.feedback: Raising the light from 60 to 80 left the rate at 8, so more light is not what this leaf is short of.
A leaf given more carbon dioxide goes on speeding up as the light rises, so there is no ceiling that every leaf shares. Something other than light is holding this one back.

questions.prompt: Equal volumes sit on either side of a membrane that the solute can cross. A student counts the solute units on each side every minute. The left reads 20, 16, 13, 12 and 12, and the right reads 4, 8, 11, 12 and 12. What do the counts show?
hints: Work out how much the left side lost in each minute.
The loss gets smaller as the difference between the sides gets smaller.

acceptedIdeas: Net movement slowed as the sides drew level and stopped when equal
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Net movement slowed as the sides drew level and stopped when equal

choices.label: Net movement slowed as the sides drew level and stopped when equal
The molecules stopped crossing as soon as the counts stopped changing
The membrane stopped letting solute through after the second minute

questions.onCorrect: The left side lost 4, 3, 1 and then 0 units: net movement shrinks with the difference, and at 12 and 12 the two directions balance.

misconceptions.feedback: At 12 and 12 molecules still cross in both directions. The counts are steady because the crossings in the two directions are equal.
The counts still changed after the second minute, from 13 to 12, and they changed by less each time because the gap was closing.

questions.prompt: An animal cell has no cell wall. It sits in pure water, which has a lower solute concentration than the cell's contents, and its membrane lets water cross but not solute. What can happen to the cell?
hints: Compare the solute concentration inside the cell with the water around it.
Water moves towards the side with the higher solute concentration.
Ask what limits the swelling of a plant cell, and whether this cell has it.

acceptedIdeas: It swells and may burst, because nothing pushes back on the water
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It swells and may burst, because nothing pushes back on the water

choices.label: It shrinks, because water moves out towards the weaker solution outside
It stays the same size, because the membrane holds water back
It swells and may burst, because nothing pushes back on the water

questions.onCorrect: Water enters towards the higher solute concentration inside the cell, and with no wall to press back, the cell can keep swelling until it bursts.

misconceptions.feedback: Water moves towards the side with the higher solute concentration, which is the inside of the cell here.
The membrane lets water cross freely, so the difference in concentration does draw water through it.

questions.prompt: Only water can cross between two compartments, at equal pressure. The left holds 6 solute units in volume 2, and the right holds 8 solute units in volume 4. Which side gains water at first?
hints: Work out each side's concentration first, as the amount of solute divided by the volume.
Only water can cross, so the solute stays where it is.
Water moves towards the side with the higher solute concentration.

acceptedIdeas: The left side, because its solute is more concentrated
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The left side, because its solute is more concentrated

choices.label: The right side, because it holds more units of solute in total
The left side, because its solute is more concentrated
Neither side, because the volumes are different

questions.onCorrect: The left side holds 6 ÷ 2 = 3 units per volume against 8 ÷ 4 = 2 on the right, so water moves towards the left.

misconceptions.feedback: Water follows concentration and not the number of units. The right side also has twice the volume, so compare the amount of solute in each unit of volume.
Unequal volumes do not stop the movement. Water moves whenever the two concentrations differ.

questions.prompt: Bacteria whose DNA has two heavy strands are moved to light material and copy their DNA once. If replication is semiconservative, what is each new molecule like?
hints: Each old strand acts as a template for a new partner.
Ask which strand each new molecule keeps and which it is given.

acceptedIdeas: It has one heavy strand and one light strand
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It has one heavy strand and one light strand

choices.label: It has two heavy strands, as the old molecule did
It has one heavy strand and one light strand
It has two light strands, because the old strands are broken down

questions.onCorrect: Each new molecule keeps one heavy strand and gets one light strand, so its density sits between the heavy and the light.

misconceptions.feedback: That would mean the old molecule is passed on whole. In semiconservative replication each old strand is separated and given a new partner.
The old strands are kept. Each serves as a template and stays paired with the new strand built on it.

questions.prompt: Bacteria with two heavy strands copy their DNA once in light material and then once more. If replication is semiconservative, how do the four molecules at the end compare?
hints: After the first copying, every molecule holds one heavy and one light strand.
In the second copying each molecule is separated into its two strands, and each strand gets a light partner.

acceptedIdeas: Two hold one heavy and one light strand, and two hold only light strands
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Two hold one heavy and one light strand, and two hold only light strands

choices.label: Two hold one heavy and one light strand, and two hold only light strands
All four hold one heavy strand and one light strand
One holds two heavy strands, and the other three hold only light strands

questions.onCorrect: The two heavy strands each sit in a different molecule, paired with a light one, and the other two molecules are all light. That gives the two bands seen after two generations.

misconceptions.feedback: There were only two heavy strands to begin with, so only two molecules can hold one. The others are built from light material.
The heavy pair is never rebuilt. Each heavy strand ends up paired with a light one, in a different molecule.

questions.prompt: A species has 4 pairs of homologous chromosomes. Ignoring crossing over, how many different combinations of chromosomes can one parent's gametes carry?
hints: Each pair lines up independently, so each pair doubles the number of combinations.
Two pairs give 4 combinations and three pairs give 8.
Double the count once for each pair.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each pair doubles the number of combinations: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16.

questions.onCorrect: Each of the 4 pairs doubles the number of combinations, so 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number for three pairs. A fourth pair doubles it again.
That is the number of pairs. Each pair doubles the number of combinations, so the count grows faster.
Thirty-two would need a fifth pair. Four pairs double the count four times.

questions.prompt: A field of insects is sprayed with a pesticide, and most of the survivors carry an allele that gives resistance to it. Where did the allele most likely come from?
hints: Mutations arise by chance, not because they are needed.
Think about whether the allele could have been in the population before the spraying.

acceptedIdeas: It arose by chance in a few insects before the spraying
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It arose by chance in a few insects before the spraying

choices.label: The pesticide caused the allele to appear in the insects it touched
Each survivor produced the allele in response to the poison
It arose by chance in a few insects before the spraying

questions.onCorrect: Mutations arise by chance, so a few insects already carried the allele. The pesticide only changed how many of each kind were left.

misconceptions.feedback: The pesticide does not aim its changes at a useful allele. Spraying decides which insects survive, and it does not make the allele.
A mutation is not made because it is needed, so no insect can produce an allele on demand.

questions.prompt: A gene has 600 bases. After a mutation it has 599. Which type of mutation was it?
hints: A substitution leaves the length the same, and the other two types change it.
Compare 599 with 600: has a base been added or lost?

acceptedIdeas: A deletion
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A deletion

choices.label: A deletion
A substitution
An insertion

questions.onCorrect: A deletion removes a base, so the gene is one base shorter, at 599.

misconceptions.feedback: A substitution replaces one base with another, so the length stays the same.
An insertion adds a base, so the length would go up.

questions.prompt: A fire leaves 5 survivors from 20 mice. Brown mice were 40% of the mice before the fire and are 60% of the survivors. Nobody measured whether brown mice survived better. What can be concluded?
hints: Think about what else besides selection can change a frequency.
A frequency change shows that something happened, but not by itself what.

acceptedIdeas: Either chance or selection could explain it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Either chance or selection could explain it

choices.label: Selection by the fire must have favoured brown mice
Either chance or selection could explain it
Neither can explain it, because the population shrank

questions.onCorrect: Either chance or selection could explain it. With no measure of how survival differed, the change alone does not show which.

misconceptions.feedback: A change in frequency shows that something happened, not what caused it.
A population can shrink and still change by chance or by selection. Size does not rule either out.

questions.prompt: In a golden meadow the share of blue beetles falls from 50% to 15% over several generations. A student wants evidence that birds are selecting against blue. Which evidence would be best?
hints: A fall in a frequency could also come from chance or from migration.
Selection needs the variants to differ in survival or reproduction in that environment.

acceptedIdeas: Equal numbers of marked blue and gold beetles set free, with more blue eaten
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Equal numbers of marked blue and gold beetles set free, with more blue eaten

choices.label: Equal numbers of marked blue and gold beetles set free, with more blue eaten
A count showing that blue beetles are now fewer than gold ones in the meadow
A second meadow where the share of blue beetles has also changed over time

questions.onCorrect: Selection has to be shown by measuring the survival or reproduction of the variants, as the bird experiments on moths did.

misconceptions.feedback: A change in frequency shows that something happened and not what caused it. Chance or migration could give the same count.
Another change in frequency has the same weakness. It shows that something happened and not what caused it.

questions.prompt: The producers in a lake hold 8000 kJ of energy, and the herbivores that eat them hold 1200 kJ. What is the transfer efficiency, as a percentage?
hints: Transfer efficiency is the fraction of the energy that is passed on to the next level.
The herbivores hold the energy that was passed on.
Divide that by the producers' energy and write the result as a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The herbivores hold 1200 ÷ 8000 = 0.15 of the producers' energy, which is 15%.

questions.onCorrect: The herbivores hold 1200 ÷ 8000 = 0.15 of the producers' energy, so the efficiency here is 15%, above the 10% rule of thumb.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the fraction. The question asks for a percentage, so multiply by 100.
That divides the producers' energy by the herbivores'. The efficiency is the energy passed on divided by the energy it came from.
That is the percentage that did not pass on. The question asks for the share that did.

questions.prompt: A population of 400 deer sits at its carrying capacity. A drought then lowers the carrying capacity to 250. What is most likely to happen over the next season?
hints: Compare the 400 deer with the new limit of 250.
A population above its carrying capacity has less food and space than it needs.
Net change is births minus deaths.

acceptedIdeas: Deaths exceed births, so the population falls towards 250
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Deaths exceed births, so the population falls towards 250

choices.label: Births and deaths stay balanced, so the population stays at 400
Deaths exceed births, so the population falls towards 250
Births exceed deaths, so the population keeps growing

questions.onCorrect: The 400 deer are above the new carrying capacity of 250, so the habitat cannot feed them all, deaths exceed births and the population falls.

misconceptions.feedback: The balance between births and deaths belongs to a population at its carrying capacity, and the capacity has just moved.
Births exceed deaths when there is spare food and room. A population above its carrying capacity has too little of both.

questions.prompt: A population has stayed close to a carrying capacity of 1,000 for many years. One year a count finds 1,300 animals. Which reading of this count is most reasonable?
hints: The S-shaped curve is a simplified model of growth.
Ask what a single count can and cannot show about the capacity.

acceptedIdeas: The population may have overshot a capacity that did not change
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The population may have overshot a capacity that did not change

choices.label: The population may have overshot a capacity that did not change
The capacity may now be 1,300, since the animals are there
The S-shaped curve may be wrong, as it did not predict 1,300

questions.onCorrect: A count above the capacity can be an overshoot, so it does not show that the capacity changed or that the model is useless.

misconceptions.feedback: The capacity can change, but a high count alone does not show that it did. Something else could account for the count.
A model that leaves things out is still useful. The S-shaped curve describes the general pattern, not every count.

questions.prompt: Across 30 woodland plots, the plots with more earthworms also have more seedlings. What follows from that observation alone?
hints: Think about what else could differ between plots with many earthworms and plots with few.
A pattern across plots does not show which way a cause runs.

acceptedIdeas: The two are associated, but soil could explain both
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The two are associated, but soil could explain both

choices.label: Earthworms must be causing the extra seedlings
Seedlings must be attracting earthworms to those plots
The two are associated, but soil could explain both

questions.onCorrect: Earthworms and seedlings are associated, but soil or moisture could account for both, so the pattern alone does not show a cause.

misconceptions.feedback: An association alone does not show cause. Plots with more earthworms may differ in soil, moisture or shade as well.
The cause could run this way, but a pattern across plots does not show which way a cause runs.

flashcards.front: What is the name of the membrane-bound compartment containing most DNA in a typical animal cell?
flashcards.back: The nucleus encloses most of the cell's DNA.

acceptedIdeas: nucleus
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The nucleus encloses most of the cell's DNA.

flashcards.front: Which organelle captures light energy in a green leaf cell?
flashcards.back: The chloroplast carries out photosynthesis; mitochondria serve a different energy role.

acceptedIdeas: chloroplast
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis; mitochondria serve a different energy role.

flashcards.front: A membrane blocks a solute completely, and one side holds far more of it than the other. Why does the solute not spread out?
flashcards.back: Diffusion needs molecules to cross. An impermeable membrane lets none through, so each side keeps the amount it started with.

flashcards.front: What word names net spreading of a freely moving substance down its concentration gradient?
flashcards.back: Diffusion produces a net flow down a concentration gradient.

acceptedIdeas: diffusion
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Diffusion produces a net flow down a concentration gradient.

flashcards.front: Name the net movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane towards the side with the higher solute concentration.
flashcards.back: Osmosis describes net water movement, not solute diffusion.

acceptedIdeas: osmosis
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Osmosis describes net water movement, not solute diffusion.

flashcards.front: Water can cross a membrane but the solute cannot, and the right side holds more solute than the left. Which way does water move, and why?
flashcards.back: From the left to the right. Only water is free to move, and it moves towards the side with the higher solute concentration.

flashcards.front: What is the energy barrier that enzymes lower?
flashcards.back: Enzymes lower activation energy; they do not supply the reaction's energy.

acceptedIdeas: activation energy
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Enzymes lower activation energy; they do not supply the reaction's energy.

flashcards.front: Why does an experiment on an enzyme need a control with no enzyme?
flashcards.back: The control shows how much product forms without the enzyme, so only the extra product in the enzyme sample can be credited to the enzyme.

flashcards.front: Which gas supplies carbon atoms that photosynthetic organisms incorporate into sugar?
flashcards.back: Carbon dioxide is a matter input; light is the energy input.

acceptedIdeas: carbon dioxide
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Carbon dioxide is a matter input; light is the energy input.

flashcards.front: In photosynthesis, what does light supply, and what do carbon dioxide and water supply?
flashcards.back: Light supplies the energy, which is stored in glucose. Carbon dioxide and water supply the matter whose atoms end up in glucose and oxygen.

flashcards.front: Name the small molecule commonly used to couple energy release to cellular work.
flashcards.back: ATP transfers energy to many energy-requiring processes.

acceptedIdeas: ATP
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: ATP transfers energy to many energy-requiring processes.

flashcards.front: Why does an experiment that measures respiration by oxygen use include a blank jar?
flashcards.back: The blank shows how much oxygen is lost for reasons that have nothing to do with the organisms. Their own use is the change in their jar minus the change in the blank.

flashcards.front: Which DNA base pairs with guanine? Give its name.
flashcards.back: Guanine pairs with cytosine (C).

acceptedIdeas: cytosine
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Guanine pairs with cytosine (C).

flashcards.front: A cell with 10 chromosomes copies its DNA. How many chromosomes does it have afterwards, and how many DNA molecules?
flashcards.back: Still 10 chromosomes, but now 20 DNA molecules, because each chromosome holds two joined sister chromatids.

flashcards.front: Why must a cell copy its DNA before mitosis?
flashcards.back: Mitosis only shares out the DNA that exists. Copying first means each daughter cell can receive a complete set.

flashcards.front: How does the number of DNA molecules in a cell change when its DNA is copied, and then when the cell divides?
flashcards.back: It doubles when the DNA is copied and halves when the cell divides, while the number of chromosomes in the cell stays the same.

flashcards.front: Why does meiosis halve the chromosome number?
flashcards.back: Fertilisation joins two gametes. If each carried the full set, the number would double in every generation, so meiosis gives each gamete half.

flashcards.front: What term describes a cell with one chromosome set?
flashcards.back: Haploid means one set; diploid means two.

acceptedIdeas: haploid
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Haploid means one set; diploid means two.

flashcards.front: In an AA × aa cross, what percentage of offspring are heterozygous under the single-gene model?
flashcards.back: Every offspring receives A from one parent and a from the other, so all are Aa.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Every offspring receives A from one parent and a from the other, so all are Aa.

flashcards.front: A plant with the dominant trait could be AA or Aa. How can a test cross tell which?
flashcards.back: Cross it with an aa plant. If any offspring show the recessive trait, the plant is Aa. If every offspring shows the dominant trait, the plant is probably AA.

flashcards.front: How does a helpful mutation become common in a population?
flashcards.back: Mutation supplies the variant by chance. Its carriers survive and reproduce more, so it makes up a larger share of each generation.

flashcards.front: A gene of 600 bases has 601 bases after a mutation. What type of mutation is this?
flashcards.back: An insertion adds a base, so the gene is one base longer.

acceptedIdeas: insertion
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An insertion adds a base, so the gene is one base longer.

flashcards.front: A variant's frequency rises in a population. Why does that alone not show that selection happened?
flashcards.back: Chance (drift) and migration can also change frequencies. You need evidence that the variants differ in survival or reproduction in that environment.

flashcards.front: What process changes variant frequencies through chance sampling rather than consistent reproductive advantage?
flashcards.back: Genetic drift changes frequencies through random sampling.

acceptedIdeas: genetic drift
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Genetic drift changes frequencies through random sampling.

flashcards.front: What ecological role is played by an organism that builds organic matter from inorganic carbon using an external energy source?
flashcards.back: A primary producer supplies organic matter to food webs.

acceptedIdeas: primary producer
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Primary producers supply organic matter to food webs.

flashcards.front: Why does a food web need a continuing supply of light even though decomposers recycle its nutrients?
flashcards.back: Matter is recycled, but energy leaves the web as heat and cannot be reused. Only producers bring in new energy, from light.

flashcards.front: Why does the energy in a food chain fall at each step up?
flashcards.back: Much of what an organism takes in is used in respiration and lost as heat, left uneaten or passed out undigested, so only a fraction reaches the next level.

flashcards.front: A consumer level gains 75 kJ at an assumed 15% efficiency. How many kJ were available one level below?
Why does a growing population slow down as it nears the carrying capacity?
flashcards.back: Food and space run short, so births tend to fall and deaths tend to rise until the two come close to balance.

flashcards.front: What term names the population size an environment can support under specified conditions in a simple growth model?
flashcards.back: Carrying capacity depends on the species and current conditions.

acceptedIdeas: carrying capacity
